_Why can a policy improve its training score while becoming less reliable on the machine?_

A learned policy acquires its behavior from the experience its training supplies, and its weights keep no record of which experience that was. Demonstrations can omit the recovery from a displaced fixture, a simulator can reward a fast approach that a real contact surface cannot tolerate, and a model pretrained on other robots can behave plausibly in conditions no one has tested on this machine. In each case the training score rises while the dependency stays hidden, so ranking candidates by score can favor the one that exploited its data or its solver. Training also fixes how long the policy takes to propose an action, and every improvement gathered on the machine itself is paid for in heat and component life. An engineer who does not understand these mechanisms cannot choose a source of experience that supports the behavior the task needs, cannot state the conditions in which a checkpoint may be trusted, and discovers each hidden dependency only when the machine meets it. Because an admitted action crosses the causal boundary and its consequences cannot be undone by another gradient update, the limits of a policy's evidence must be established before it is allowed to propose motion.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare training regimes, from behavioral cloning to post-training a pretrained generalist, by the experience they supply and the physical dependencies they leave in the policy
- Diagnose the separate risks of averaging valid action choices and drifting beyond demonstrated states
- Calculate whether an action decoder fits its proposal deadline and identify the required execution safeguards
- Evaluate simulator mismatch and distinguish parameter variation from missing mechanisms or unavailable observations
- Bound real-machine adaptation by physical exposure, residual authority, and regression evidence
- Construct a policy manifest that confines a candidate's declared operating region to its documented support

:::

## Dual Failure Modes of Policy Training {#sec-training-policy-synthesis}

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-latch-contact-deadline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LATCH CONTACT DEADLINE AT THE GUARDED AND FAST APPROACHES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The chapter opener, the decoder run-time cost, the contact-exploit
# │          section, and the latch policy manifest's declared ODD.
# │ Goal: Show why the latch policy's declared ODD admits only the guarded
# │       approach: at the fast approach the contact deadline barely exceeds
# │       the tripwire-to-brake response after threshold accumulation.
# │ Show: setpoint and chunk periods, both approach speeds, latch limit, contact-loop
# │       response, threshold and brake-onset times, and the two deadlines.
# │ How: F = k*v*t, so t_yield = F_lim / (k*v) (calc_contact_yield_deadline);
# │      every input from RM / AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_contact_yield_deadline

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchContactDeadline:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen (chunk-policy setpoint period)
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (chunk-policy renewal rate)
    k_plate = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative (strike-plate contact stiffness)
    v_guarded = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative (guarded, demonstrated approach speed)
    v_fast = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (unsupported fast approach speed)
    f_lim = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative (latch force limit)
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative (contact tripwire force)
    t_contact_loop = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (tripwire-detection-to-brake-onset response time)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_chunk = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)  # chunk renewal period, the asynchronous inference deadline
    t_yield_guarded = calc_contact_yield_deadline(f_lim, k_plate, v_guarded).to(millisecond)
    t_yield_fast = calc_contact_yield_deadline(f_lim, k_plate, v_fast).to(millisecond)
    t_trip_fast = (f_trip / (k_plate * v_fast)).to(millisecond)
    t_trip_guarded = (f_trip / (k_plate * v_guarded)).to(millisecond)
    t_brake_fast = (t_trip_fast + t_contact_loop).to(millisecond)
    t_brake_guarded = (t_trip_guarded + t_contact_loop).to(millisecond)
    fast_margin_ratio = (t_yield_fast / t_brake_fast).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_left_fast = (t_yield_fast - t_brake_fast).to(millisecond)
    t_left_guarded = (t_yield_guarded - t_brake_guarded).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"setpoint period {t_step}")  # M5: 2 steps per renewal
    check(
        abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"chunk period {t_chunk}"
    )  # 25 ms and 50 ms are hand-drawn in fig06_privileged_distillation.svg
    check(t_chunk > t_step, "the chunk period must exceed the setpoint period that paces playback")
    check(abs(t_yield_guarded.to(millisecond).magnitude - 8.333) < 0.001, f"guarded deadline {t_yield_guarded}")
    check(abs(v_guarded.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, f"guarded approach {v_guarded}")
    check(abs(v_fast.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, f"fast approach {v_fast}")
    check(abs(f_lim.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"latch limit {f_lim}")
    check(abs(t_left_fast.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.125) < 1e-9, f"time left at fast approach {t_left_fast}")
    check(abs(t_yield_fast.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, f"fast deadline {t_yield_fast}")
    check(abs(t_contact_loop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"contact loop {t_contact_loop}")
    check(0 * newton < f_trip < f_lim, "tripwire must precede the force limit")
    check(abs(t_trip_fast.magnitude - 0.375) < 1e-9, f"fast tripwire crossing {t_trip_fast}")
    check(abs(t_trip_guarded.magnitude - 1.25) < 1e-9, f"guarded tripwire crossing {t_trip_guarded}")
    check(abs(t_brake_fast.magnitude - 2.375) < 1e-9, f"fast brake onset {t_brake_fast}")
    check(abs(t_brake_guarded.magnitude - 3.25) < 1e-9, f"guarded brake onset {t_brake_guarded}")
    check(abs(t_left_guarded.magnitude - 5.083333333) < 1e-8, f"guarded time left {t_left_guarded}")
    check(1.0 < fast_margin_ratio < 1.1, "fast deadline must sit barely above brake onset")
    check(t_left_guarded > 2 * t_contact_loop, "guarded approach must leave several response intervals after brake onset")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_guarded_str = fmt_velocity(v_guarded, precision=2)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, precision=2)
    f_lim_str = fmt_force(f_lim, precision=0)
    t_contact_loop_str = fmt_latency(t_contact_loop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_yield_guarded_str = fmt_latency(t_yield_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
    t_yield_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_yield_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_trip_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_trip_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
    t_trip_guarded_str = fmt_latency(t_trip_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_brake_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_brake_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
    t_brake_guarded_str = fmt_latency(t_brake_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_left_fast_str = fmt_latency(t_left_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
    t_left_guarded_str = fmt_latency(t_left_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=3)
```

A robot arm executing a learned trajectory can track every waypoint cleanly across hundreds of simulation episodes and still arrive at its first physical deployment with no evidence about whether it will fracture a latch. In classical robotics, control design begins with an explicit analytical model of the plant: engineers write down kinematic equations, inertia matrices, stability margins, and torque limits where they can be systematically inspected and verified. A learned neural policy, in contrast, derives its behavior entirely from its training distribution, setting network weights from empirical experience to map physical observations to proposed control actions. That experience may arrive as teleoperated demonstrations, recorded operational logs, rollouts inside a parallel physics simulator, trial-and-error interactions on physical hardware, or pretrained representations imported from foundation models. Although empirical data makes complex manipulation tractable, it also embeds unstated dynamic assumptions directly into the model weights, leaving no explicit record of which operating regimes the policy can safely navigate.

The central engineering question in embodied policy training is therefore not which regime achieves the highest optimization score, but which physical behaviors the training experience supports, and at what operational cost. Four quantities decide the answer. The first is coverage, because a policy is supported only in the states its experience actually visited, which is why the provenance record of @sec-data-schema lists its known absences beside its demonstrated cells. The second is inference latency, because a policy that evaluates too slowly misses its control deadline, however good its proposed trajectories are. The third is hardware cost, since experience gathered on the machine consumes machine hours, heats motor windings, and wears drivetrains. The fourth is fidelity, because synthetic experience from simulation scales across parallel accelerators but is only as faithful as the integrator and contact solver that produced it. A checkpoint's policy manifest (@sec-training-policy-manifest) records all four, and its declared operational design domain (ODD) is the part of the task's scenario table that the checkpoint's evidence supports. Two candidate latch policies show why a clean training curve does not establish physical viability.

Consider the cage-door latch task introduced in @sec-data-endogenous-experience, where two learned controllers both succeed under nominal warehouse conditions yet each carries a hidden dependency that physical hardware can expose, for different mechanical reasons. Both controllers share the same real-time execution model: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning], a chunk-policy architecture that generates open-loop action sequences in a single decoder pass. The first candidate, `latch-bc-01`, was trained via supervised behavioral cloning on teleoperated door-opening demonstrations. The second candidate, `latch-sim-02`, is a distilled student policy: a reinforcement learning teacher was first trained inside a massively parallel physics simulator with full access to privileged state variables, after which `latch-sim-02`, initialized from `latch-bc-01`, learned through distillation to replicate the teacher's actions using only onboard sensor streams (@sec-training-privileged-distillation).

Both candidates inherit the absence list of the baseline archive. Its demonstrations characterize only the nominal strike plate at a guarded approach velocity, so a displaced plate and a faster approach are both recorded as known absences, and each candidate meets one of them. While behavioral cloning must interpolate between these discrete demonstrations to form coherent trajectory proposals, interactive learning in simulation can explore novel state-action pairs. However, the validity of that synthetic exploration depends entirely on how accurately the simulated mechanics mirror the physical plant. Selecting a training regime is therefore an architectural decision that dictates which unverified assumptions must be empirically audited before a checkpoint is permitted to command actuators.

In this illustrative comparison, at the nominal strike plate and the guarded approach speed of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded_str`, both policies open the door. Their failure modes diverge once physical deployment departs from that single nominal operating point:

1. **Missing recovery experience**: When a sagging door places the strike plate off nominal, `latch-bc-01` encounters observations outside its training distribution. Because behavioral cloning minimizes supervised prediction error across the recorded demonstrations, the training loss supplies no direct supervision at unvisited recovery states, although updates to shared weights can still change the actions predicted there. When confronted with unfamiliar observations, the network still emits action setpoints, but those ungrounded commands drive the manipulator further off course. Trajectory errors compound at each `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` setpoint tick until the gripper binds against the strike plate's chamfered edge. The root bottleneck is the absence of corrective recovery trajectories in the training distribution, rather than model capacity.
2. **Misleading simulated contact**: In contrast, `latch-sim-02` is at risk on the nominal strike plate itself. Its simulator models contact dynamics using a compliant penalty spring[^fn-penalty-contact-model] ($\NormalContactForce = \PenaltyContactStiffness \PenetrationDepth + \PenaltyContactDamping \PenetrationRate$), where surface penetration $\PenetrationDepth$ and penetration rate $\PenetrationRate$ govern the contact force. Because this numerical spring yields far more compliance than a physical steel plate, the simulated impact at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_fast_str` peaks well under the latch's `{python} LatchContactDeadline.f_lim_str` limit. The teacher's training reward paid for opening the door quickly and carried no term for contact force, so nothing in training charged for an aggressive approach, and the optimizer exploited the contact model to shave cycle time off each episode. The reinforcement learning teacher converges on an aggressive plunge, and policy distillation faithfully transfers that shortcut into the student. Whether the plunge breaks the real latch depends on how stiff the arm side of the contact is, a quantity nothing in training measured.

[^fn-penalty-contact-model]: **Kelvin-Voigt Contact**: A linear spring and damper in parallel produce a force jump at first touch, because the damping term acts on the full approach velocity at zero penetration, and a pulling, "sticky" force as the bodies separate, because the damping term then outweighs the vanishing spring term. @hunt1975coefficient scaled the damping with penetration to remove both artifacts. A policy trained against the linear model therefore meets its least faithful forces at contact onset and at release, the two events a latch opening depends on. \index{Contact model!Kelvin-Voigt}

A contact-force budget demonstrates why the simulated benchmark score cannot be trusted on hardware. In the rigid-arm, constant-drive estimate, the physical strike plate's stiffness sets the force rise. At the unbraked approach velocity of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_fast_str`, force reaches the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.f_lim_str` limit in `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_yield_fast_str` after touch. The tripwire fires at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_trip_fast_str`; the subsequent `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_contact_loop_str` response places brake onset at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_brake_fast_str`, leaving only `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_left_fast_str` before the constant-drive ramp reaches the limit. That interval is not a stopping certificate. @Sec-training-contact-exploit derives the timeline alongside the passive impact forces; sanctioning the fast plunge would require physical deceleration evidence that this simulation-only training process cannot establish.

Both failures expose critical dependencies hidden from validation loss and episodic reward: behavioral cloning depends on demonstrated recovery distributions, while simulation-to-real transfer depends on faithful contact and stiffness dynamics. Selecting a policy training regime therefore requires matching the physical properties of the training source to the mechanical demands of the operational task. Whichever regime produced it, a learned checkpoint sits above the proposal boundary as an unprivileged proposal generator. Achieving safe and reliable manipulation requires action proposals that respect the machine's actuator dynamics, contact deadlines, and physical safety envelopes as rigorously as they pursue the nominal task objective, and comparing the five regimes that can generate those proposals clarifies what each source of experience buys and what it leaves unverified.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The proposal boundary, under which a learned proposer holds no authority until an independent permission path admits its command, is established in @sec-boundary-machine-model.
:::

## Policy Training Regimes {#sec-training-synthesis-regimes}

When `latch-bc-01` binds against a sagged strike plate and `latch-sim-02` plunges into the nominal plate at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_fast_str`, neither failure can be repaired simply by training the same network for more epochs on the same dataset. Fixing an unvisited recovery state or an exploited contact solver requires changing the experience the learner sees. Training a control policy for the latch task can draw on five sources of experience: teleoperated door openings, logged archives of imperfect or scripted trajectories, a physics simulator of the door and cage, direct physical trial on the arm itself, and a generalist foundation checkpoint pretrained across multi-robot corpora. Each source buys distinct sensorimotor capabilities at a characteristic physical cost and leaves its own failure mode behind (@tbl-06-regimes). Behavioral cloning, batch offline reinforcement learning, and supervised post-training extract control policies from recorded datasets without runtime exploration, whereas online trial, conducted in simulation or on the physical mechanism, generates new interactions under closed-loop feedback. Comparing how those regimes evaluate and update actions begins with the reward quantities that score closed-loop behavior over an episode.

| Policy Training Regime             | Core Purchased Capability                                                                                        | Data & Compute Budget                                                   | Sample Efficiency & Scale                                              | Hardware Safety & Wear Risk                                                                          | Dominant Failure Mode & Interceptor                                                                                                                           |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Behavioral Cloning (BC)**        | Imitates attributable expert actions                                                                             | Expert collection, curation, and supervised optimization                | Limited by coverage and operator availability                          | Optimization adds no physical exploration; collection still incurs exposure                          | Mode averaging and missing recovery. Multimodal decoding and new expert labels address training; qualified state and action limits bound execution.           |
| **Offline / Batch RL**             | Uses rewards to select behavior from heterogeneous logs                                                          | Logged transitions with rewards and state-action coverage               | Reuses recorded experience without new online trials                   | Optimization adds no exploration; the archive inherits collection risks                              | Unsupported action values. Conservative objectives reduce optimism; independent action limits remain necessary.                                               |
| **Sim-to-Real RL**                 | Explores behavior through simulated interaction; a privileged teacher can be distilled into a deployable student | Parallel rollout compute plus physical calibration and transfer tests   | Throughput depends on task, solver, and hardware                       | Simulation avoids training wear; physical probing and deployment still incur exposure                | Solver exploitation and omitted mechanisms. Paired probes qualify the simulator; approach and force limits need their own response evidence.                  |
| **Residual RL & Real Fine-Tuning** | Adapts to local physical mismatch                                                                                | Machine interaction, resets, cooling, and regression testing            | Physical trials make sample efficiency consequential                   | Contact loads and thermal exposure accumulate during adaptation                                      | Local improvement with regression elsewhere. Independent residual gates limit authority; combined-controller tests assess the change.                         |
| **Pretrain & Post-Train**          | Starts from a generalist checkpoint's broad competence and adapts it to the task with demonstrations or reward   | A base checkpoint trained elsewhere, task data, and fine-tuning compute | Task data needs shrink when the base already represents related skills | Supervised post-training adds no exploration; RL post-training adds the exposure of its own rollouts | Borrowed competence mistaken for evidence, and forgetting. Support comes only from the task data join; regression tests cover what post-training may disturb. |

: **Comparative trade-off matrix across policy training regimes**: The five regimes compared are behavioral cloning, offline reinforcement learning, sim-to-real reinforcement learning, residual RL/fine-tuning, and post-training of a pretrained generalist policy. Columns separate the capability sought, the resources that determine its cost, and the remaining failure mechanism. Training remedies and physical execution safeguards have different roles; neither supplies the other's evidence. {#tbl-06-regimes tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

### The latch task as a reward problem {#sec-training-rl-primer}

A reward function that pays a policy for opening the cage door and penalizes each control step for elapsed time without charging for contact force will train the arm to slam into the strike plate, because every millisecond shaved off the approach increases the episode's score. Even behavioral cloning, which uses no reward during training, has its failures measured in the quantities that a reward problem defines: the states a policy visits, the return it earns over an episode, and the value of one action against another. Posing the latch mechanism as a discrete-time optimal control problem makes those quantities concrete and shows how an omitted force penalty or a discount factor mis-scaled against the control rate distorts learned behavior.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-latch-reward-problem
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE LATCH AS A MARKOV DECISION PROCESS: EPISODE LENGTH AND DISCOUNT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-training-rl-primer; the episode length is reused by the
# │          hardware trial calendar in @sec-training-learning-by-trial.
# │ Goal: Show that the discount factor acts per decision, so its horizon in
# │       seconds depends on the machine's setpoint step.
# │ Show: decisions per opening, the terminal reward's weight at the first
# │       decision, the effective horizon in steps and seconds, and the
# │       smallest discount that keeps half the terminal weight.
# │ How: n = t_rollout / t_step; w = gamma^n; horizon = 1 / (1 - gamma);
# │      gamma_half = 0.5^(1/n). Step from RM; rollout and gamma are chosen.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchRewardProblem:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen (setpoint step, one decision)
    t_rollout = 8.0 * second  # category: illustrative (autonomous contact phase of one opening, not the 25 s collection attempt of @sec-data)
    gamma = 0.99  # category: chosen (a common discount factor)
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative (contact tripwire on the latch)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_decisions = round((t_rollout / t_step).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    w_terminal = gamma**n_decisions
    horizon_steps = 1 / (1 - gamma)
    horizon_time = (horizon_steps * t_step).to(second)
    gamma_half = 0.5 ** (1 / n_decisions)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"setpoint step {t_step}")
    check(n_decisions == 320, f"decisions per opening {n_decisions}")
    check(abs(w_terminal - 0.0402) < 1e-3, f"terminal weight {w_terminal}")
    check(abs(horizon_steps - 100.0) < 1e-6, f"effective horizon {horizon_steps}")
    check(abs(horizon_time.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, f"horizon in seconds {horizon_time}")
    check(horizon_time < t_rollout, "the effective horizon must be shorter than one opening")
    check(gamma < gamma_half < 1, "keeping half the terminal weight must need a larger discount")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, f"tripwire {f_trip}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_rollout_str = fmt_time(t_rollout, second, precision=0)
    n_decisions_str = fmt_int(n_decisions)
    gamma_str = fmt(gamma, precision=2)
    w_terminal_str = fmt(w_terminal, precision=2)
    horizon_steps_str = fmt_int(horizon_steps)
    horizon_time_str = fmt_time(horizon_time, second, precision=1)
    gamma_half_str = fmt(gamma_half, precision=4)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
```

A **Markov decision process** (MDP)\index{Markov decision process}[^fn-mdp-bellman-origin] describes a task by its state $\DecisionProcessState_{t}$, its action $\ContinuousActionVector_{t}$, a transition $\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \ContinuousActionVector_{t})$ that the physics supplies, and a scalar reward $\Reward(\DecisionProcessState_{t}, \ContinuousActionVector_{t})$ that the engineer writes. For the latch, the state holds the gripper pose, the plate position, and the measured contact force. The action is the setpoint the chunk policy emits every `{python} LatchRewardProblem.t_step_str`. An episode is one opening, `{python} LatchRewardProblem.t_rollout_str` of autonomous contact-phase motion, or `{python} LatchRewardProblem.n_decisions_str` decisions. A reward that states what the task values and what it must avoid is
$$\Reward_t = \DoorOpenReward\,\mathbb{1}[\text{door open at } \ControlStepIndex] - \ExcessForcePenaltyWeight \max\left(0, \LatchContactForce_t - \ContactTripwireForce\right) - \StepTimePenalty,$$ {#eq-training-latch-reward}
where $\ContactTripwireForce$ is the `{python} LatchRewardProblem.f_trip_str` contact tripwire, the force threshold that triggers the machine's qualified collection response (set below the latch's damage limit), $\ExcessForcePenaltyWeight$ is a weight in reward per newton of excess force, and $\StepTimePenalty$ charges each step for slowness. The weights make the terms commensurable, and choosing them is a design decision that the policy manifest records. Dropping the force term, as the simulator teacher of `latch-sim-02` did, leaves only the time term to shape the approach, and the time term rewards every millisecond an aggressive plunge saves. On hardware the success indicator must itself be measured, by a latch sensor or a learned classifier, and every error in that measurement is a surface the optimizer can exploit. When engineers introduce auxiliary rewards to guide exploration toward that success indicator, adding a potential difference $\DiscountFactor\ShapingPotential(\NextDecisionProcessState) - \ShapingPotential(\DecisionProcessState)$ provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged, and without further assumptions about the task it is the only added term that does [@ng1999policy]. Any other shaping term can change what is optimal.

[^fn-mdp-bellman-origin]: **Markov Decision Process**: @bellman1957dynamic formulated sequential decisions under uncertainty with the dynamic-programming recursion that @eq-training-bellman restates, and @howard1960dynamic supplied policy iteration to solve them. The formalism came from operations research and optimal control decades before reinforcement learning adopted it, which is why the cost-to-go translation below is an identity rather than an analogy, and why a control engineer's tools for that recursion apply to a learned policy's value function. \index{Markov decision process!origin}

A **policy**\index{Policy!stochastic} $\Policy(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \DecisionProcessState)$ is a distribution over actions, and its **return** from step $\ControlStepIndex$ is $\DiscountedReturn_t = \sum_{j \ge 0} \DiscountFactor^\DiscountedReturnStepOffset \Reward_{\ControlStepIndex+\DiscountedReturnStepOffset}$ with discount factor $\DiscountFactor \in [0, 1)$. Because $\DiscountFactor$ applies once per decision, its horizon is measured in control steps, not seconds. At $\DiscountFactor =$ `{python} LatchRewardProblem.gamma_str` and one decision every `{python} LatchRewardProblem.t_step_str`, the door-open reward earned at the end of an opening reaches the first decision with weight `{python} LatchRewardProblem.w_terminal_str`, and the effective horizon $1/(1-\DiscountFactor)$ of `{python} LatchRewardProblem.horizon_steps_str` steps spans only `{python} LatchRewardProblem.horizon_time_str`. For the terminal success to keep half its weight across the whole opening, $\DiscountFactor$ must be at least `{python} LatchRewardProblem.gamma_half_str`. Changing the setpoint rate without re-deriving $\DiscountFactor$ therefore changes the task horizon in seconds. Training a policy means choosing $\ModelParameters$ to maximize the **objective** $\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{\Policy}[\DiscountedReturn_0]$, the return expected over whole episodes that start from the task's initial states. It is a return to maximize, where the $\Glyph{J}(\pi)$ of @eq-data-quadratic-drift was an expected cost to minimize.

Two expectations of the return organize every reinforcement learning method. The **state value**\index{Value function!state} $\PolicyRemainingReturn(\DecisionProcessState) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\DiscountedReturn_t \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t} = \DecisionProcessState]$ is the return expected from $\DecisionProcessState$ when following $\pi$. The **action value** $\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\DiscountedReturn_t \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t} = \DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector_t = \ContinuousActionVector]$ is the return expected after taking $\ContinuousActionVector$ first and following $\pi$ thereafter. Both obey the one-step **Bellman relation**\index{Bellman relation}
$$\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) = \Reward(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) + \DiscountFactor\, \mathbb{E}_{\NextDecisionProcessState \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution,\ \SuccessorActionVector \sim \pi}\left[ \PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\NextDecisionProcessState, \SuccessorActionVector) \right], \qquad \PolicyRemainingReturn(\DecisionProcessState) = \mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \sim \pi}\left[ \PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) \right].$$ {#eq-training-bellman}
The **advantage**\index{Advantage function} $\PolicyHistoryAdvantage(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) = \PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\DecisionProcessState, \ContinuousActionVector) - \PolicyRemainingReturn(\DecisionProcessState)$ measures whether an action does better or worse than the policy's usual choice from that state. At the plate, an approach has positive advantage only if its expected return exceeds the policy's usual choice. A force penalty can make a plunge less attractive, but the sign still depends on the reward weights, completion probability, and baseline policy.

Readers from control have met these objects under other names. With stage cost $\ell = -\Reward$, the value is the negated **cost-to-go**\index{Cost-to-go!relation to value function}, $\CostToGo(\DecisionProcessState) = -\ExpectedRemainingReturn(\DecisionProcessState)$, and @eq-training-bellman is the dynamic-programming recursion. (Control texts write the cost-to-go as $\Glyph{J}$; this chapter reserves $\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters)$ for the expected return a learner maximizes.) For linear dynamics in the plant state $\MechanicalPlantState$ and quadratic cost, that recursion has the closed-form solution $\CostToGo(\MechanicalPlantState) = \MechanicalPlantState^\top \LqrCostToGoMatrix \MechanicalPlantState$ that the linear-quadratic regulator computes from a Riccati equation (@sec-appendix-control-lqr). Reinforcement learning keeps the recursion and changes the estimation problem: the dynamics are unknown, so $\ExpectedRemainingReturn$ and $\ExpectedHistoryActionReturn$ are fitted from sampled transitions instead of solved from a model.

These quantities organize policy learning along two axes, what is estimated and where the data comes from. Fitting $\ExpectedHistoryActionReturn$ over an immutable logged archive to select high-value actions is **offline reinforcement learning** (@sec-training-offline-rl). Generating fresh rollouts from $\Policy$, using each batch for a few updates, and shifting probability toward positive-advantage actions is on-policy **policy-gradient** optimization (@sec-training-learning-by-trial). Between the two, value-based methods also run online and off-policy. The machine keeps collecting experience, but each transition enters a replay buffer and is reused across many value updates, which is how the demonstration-seeded methods of @sec-training-real-world-rl learn in hours. The value-fitting and policy-gradient derivations behind these approaches appear in @sec-appendix-ml-affordances. Before paying the reward-design or physical trial cost of those methods, however, the simplest training regime bypasses value estimation altogether and fits a policy directly to the expert setpoints the collection campaign already recorded.

### Behavioral cloning and its action targets {#sec-training-behavioral-cloning}

**Behavioral cloning**\index{Behavioral cloning} avoids designing a reward for the nominal opening by framing policy training, as ALVINN first did for road following [@pomerleau1989alvinn], as supervised regression or classification over a collected dataset of expert state-action pairs $\DemonstrationDataset = \{(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ContinuousActionVector_t)\}$. On a physical machine, however, the four-stream action taps record both the operator's mapped setpoints and the setpoints the permission path actually admitted:
$$\IntentDemonstrationDataset = \left\{ \left(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \NominalCommandWindow\right) \right\} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \VerifiedDemonstrationDataset = \left\{ \left(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \CertifiedCommandWindow\right) \right\}$$
The mapped setpoint $\NominalControlCommand$ is the record at the mapped-command tap $\MappedCommandTap$, and the admitted setpoint $\CertifiedControlAction$ is the record at the enforced-command tap $\EnforcedCommandTap$. @Sec-data-four-stream-action-tap develops what each tap teaches a policy. In brief, cloning admitted setpoints couples the weights to one permission path's intervention profile and tuning—so an uncurated policy can learn to steer straight into the safety clamps and rely on the hardware filter to bend its commands back onto the latch—whereas cloning mapped setpoints keeps intent separate from enforcement at the price of more frequent runtime interventions, and neither tap yields an expert target without curation. The latch campaign took the mapped command as its target wherever the permission path admitted it unchanged, so `latch-bc-01` clones $\NominalControlCommand$ on those steps and treats every modified command as an attributed intervention.

Whichever tap supplies the target, the training loss compares the proposed setpoints with the recorded ones, over a single step or over the $\ActionChunkHorizon$-step sequence that @sec-training-action-chunking calls a chunk. Because this loss penalizes only the discrepancy between the commanded action and the recorded demonstration at observed states, the training objective does not evaluate task completion, terminal cost, or the stability of the closed-loop dynamical system. It fits actions to observations only, and that point-by-point fit breaks down at a single observation whenever demonstrators solve the same physical geometry in more than one valid way.

### Mode averaging when demonstrations split {#sec-training-multimodality-breakdown}

A mobile manipulator trained with least-squares regression on demonstrations that pass left of a central structural column half the time and right of it the other half will steer straight down the center line into the column. Each human teleoperator trajectory in the recorded archive $\DemonstrationDataset$ is dynamically valid and collision-free, and not a single demonstration drives into the obstacle, yet a deterministic point-regression policy proposes the one path that every demonstrator avoided.

Under empirical mean squared error ($\ell_2$) loss, a deterministic behavioral cloning network cannot represent both modes for the same observation $\MultimodalObservation_{t}$ and instead optimizes:
$$\MeanSquaredErrorCloningLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ContinuousActionVector) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \left\| \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t}) - \ContinuousActionVector \right\|_2^2 \right].$$
The theoretical minimizer of this objective is the conditional expectation of the action distribution (derived formally in @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal):
$$\pi^*(\MultimodalObservation_{t}) = \arg\min_{\CandidateActionVector} \int \|\CandidateActionVector - \ContinuousActionVector\|_2^2\,\DemonstrationArchiveActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t})\,\DerivativeOperator\ContinuousActionVector = \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}] = \int \ContinuousActionVector\,\DemonstrationArchiveActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t})\,\DerivativeOperator\ContinuousActionVector.$$ {#eq-training-mse-minimizer}
In conventional computer vision, predicting the conditional mean of ambiguous pixel targets generates blurry, averaged textures; in natural language processing, it produces diffused semantic embeddings. In Physical AI, however, the conditional expectation of two collision-free evasion commands (such as $\LeftEvasionAction = [\BaseForwardSpeed, +\YawRate]^\top$ and $\RightEvasionAction = [\BaseForwardSpeed, -\YawRate]^\top$, where $\BaseForwardSpeed$ is forward linear speed and $\YawRate$ is angular yaw rate) evaluates to:
$$\mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}] = \frac{1}{2}\LeftEvasionAction + \frac{1}{2}\RightEvasionAction = \left[ \BaseForwardSpeed, 0.0 \right]^\top.$$
The regression mean proposes forward motion with zero lateral evasion. If admitted unchanged, that proposal heads straight into the central obstacle.[^fn-jensen-inequality-plant]

[^fn-jensen-inequality-plant]: **Jensen's Inequality**: The averaged action fails even where it happens to be admissible, because a nonlinear plant does not map the mean action to the mean outcome. In general $\mathbb{E}[\PlantOutcomeFunction(\ContinuousActionVector)] \ne \PlantOutcomeFunction(\mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector])$, and for a convex $\PlantOutcomeFunction$ Jensen's inequality fixes the sign of the gap. Contact and friction are the most nonlinear parts of a manipulator's plant, so a regression mean that looks like a compromise between two good demonstrations can produce a contact state that neither demonstration visited. \index{Mode averaging!Jensen's inequality}

This invalid proposal is not caused by an optimization pathology, insufficient model capacity, or dataset scarcity. It is the exact minimizer of a point-regression loss over a multimodal distribution. Viewed as a function of the proposed action, the expected loss is a bowl with a single bottom at the mean, and that bottom sits in the zero-density gap between the two demonstrated modes ($\DemonstrationArchiveActionDistribution(\mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector\mid\MultimodalObservation_{t}] \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) \approx 0$). The statement concerns the optimal output, not whether optimizing the network's weights is convex.

::: {#dfn-training-mode-averaging .callout-definition title="Mode averaging"}

***Mode averaging***\index{Mode averaging!definition} is the failure in which a policy trained with a point-regression loss on demonstrations that contain several valid actions for one observation proposes their conditional mean, an action that lies between the demonstrated modes and that no demonstrator chose.

1.  **Significance**: More data, capacity, or training moves the output toward the mean, not away from it. Two equally weighted evasions at $\pm\YawRate$ average to zero yaw, a proposal aimed at the obstacle both demonstrations avoided, and it reaches the permission path as a smooth, confident command whose consequence cannot be undone once admitted.
2.  **Distinction**: Mode averaging concerns the action chosen at one observation; compounding error concerns the states that successive actions reach. A multimodal decoder removes the first and does nothing for the second, which needs recovery experience.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reading a low validation loss as evidence against averaging. The mean minimizes squared error on held-out demonstrations drawn from the same modes, so a regression head can score best on its split and still propose the invalid middle action at every bifurcation.

:::

Changing the regression penalty does not by itself represent alternative actions. Mean absolute error ($\ell_1$) admits conditional medians, while Huber loss limits the influence of large residuals, so neither guarantees a unique, coherent route through a multimodal demonstration distribution. Instead, the decoder must represent the alternatives, and execution must maintain a consistent choice across successive observations.

Several decoder families represent these alternatives at different computational costs. **Mixture Density Networks (MDNs)**[^fn-mdn-inverse-model] parameterize a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM): $\DemonstrationArchiveActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) = \sum_{\MixtureComponentIndex=1}^{\MixtureComponentCount} \pi_\MixtureComponentIndex(\MultimodalObservation_{t}) \GaussianDistribution\left(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MixtureComponentMean(\MultimodalObservation_{t}), \MixtureComponentCovariance(\MultimodalObservation_{t})\right)$, in which $\pi_\MixtureComponentIndex$ is the weight of component $\MixtureComponentIndex$ (not the policy), and $\MixtureComponentMean$ and $\MixtureComponentCovariance$ are its mean (not a friction coefficient) and covariance. They produce mixture parameters in one forward pass, but training must prevent covariance collapse ($\MixtureComponentCovariance \to \ZeroMatrix$) and loss of less frequent modes, which makes the component count and covariance representation consequential for high-dimensional chunks ($\ChunkActionDimension = \ActionDimension \times \ActionChunkHorizon$). Energy-based models instead score each candidate with a learned energy and must search for a low-energy action, so their iteration budget, rather than a head of fixed size, must fit the proposal deadline.

[^fn-mdn-inverse-model]: **Mixture Density Network**: @bishop1994mixture proposed it for inverse problems, whose inputs admit several valid outputs, and demonstrated it on the inverse kinematics of a robot arm, where one hand position has two joint solutions and least-squares regression returns their invalid average. The mobile manipulator's two routes around the column are the same problem, met three decades later in action space, which is why the remedy is still a change of output distribution rather than a larger network. \index{Mixture density network!inverse problems}

Generative architectures, including diffusion models [@ho2020denoising] and flow matching [@lipman2022flow], offer another way to represent $\DemonstrationArchiveActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t})$ by training a model to refine a noisy action candidate toward the learned distribution rather than returning its conditional mean. Sampling can then select a coherent demonstration mode ($\LeftEvasionAction$ or $\RightEvasionAction$). Although representing multiple modes resolves the averaging problem, a generated candidate can still violate clearance or actuator constraints, so the permission path must check it before execution.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-mode-chatter
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MODE-BOUNDARY CHATTER: LOOP RATES AND OPPOSING EFFORTS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The chattering paragraph of @sec-training-multimodality-breakdown.
# │ Goal: Keep the illustrative loop-rate band and the opposing joint efforts
# │       of the chatter example out of hand-typed prose.
# │ Show: the feedback-loop rate band and the two opposing torques.
# │ How: No arithmetic; every value is an illustrative scenario input.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import hertz

class ModeChatter:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    f_loop_lo = 50.0 * hertz  # category: illustrative (feedback-loop rate, low end)
    f_loop_hi = 100.0 * hertz  # category: illustrative (feedback-loop rate, high end)
    tau_opp = 10.0 * newton * meter  # category: illustrative (opposing joint effort magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(f_loop_lo < f_loop_hi, "the loop-rate band must be ordered")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_loop_lo_num_str = fmt(f_loop_lo.to(hertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    f_loop_hi_str = fmt_frequency(f_loop_hi, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    tau_opp_str = fmt_torque(tau_opp, precision=0)
```

A mode boundary in a single-step Markov policy can also produce high-frequency temporal chattering. In a `{python} ModeChatter.f_loop_lo_num_str`--`{python} ModeChatter.f_loop_hi_str` feedback loop, microscopic sensor noise drives consecutive observations back and forth across the mode boundary, causing a single-step controller mapping $\MultimodalObservation_{t} \to \ContinuousActionVector_{t}$ to alternate between opposing actuator efforts (for example, +`{python} ModeChatter.tau_opp_str` and −`{python} ModeChatter.tau_opp_str`). This alternation excites drivetrain resonances, accelerates gear tooth fatigue, and drives motor winding temperatures toward their thermal limit. Even when a multimodal decoder commits to one route and avoids chattering across the boundary, however, a second imitation failure emerges as soon as a small tracking error pushes the robot outside the states the demonstrators visited.

### Compounding errors and recovery experience {#sec-training-recovery-experience}

A policy can choose a coherent route around the column and still drift into states its demonstrations never covered. Mode averaging concerns the action selected at one observation; compounding error concerns the observations created by successive actions. Keeping these failures separate prevents a richer action decoder from being mistaken for recovery experience. Cloning fits actions only at the states the demonstrators visited, whereas deployment visits the states the policy's own actions create, and a fixed archive holds no example of the states the policy's execution errors reach. In continuous physical state spaces, this decoupling produces **compounding covariate shift**, which is the second law (endogenous data, principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}) acting on a fixed archive.

@Sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability bounds the price of this shift: fixed-archive cloning admits a worst-case imitation cost that grows as $\BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError$ over an $\BehaviorCloningHorizon$-step horizon (@eq-data-quadratic-drift). That bound counts accumulated task cost, not displacement, and the physical drift behind it depends on what the action commands and on the feedback below the policy. A persistent error in a commanded velocity integrates once into position, so the drift grows linearly in time; a persistent error in a commanded torque integrates twice, so it grows quadratically. A velocity-level policy also sits above a joint velocity loop that rejects load disturbances between its decisions, whereas a torque-level policy has no such loop beneath it and must supply every correction itself. Offline validation on demonstration splits measures prediction accuracy on the demonstrated distribution; recovery after displacement requires additional closed-loop evidence.

The regime that supplies that recovery experience is interactive imitation learning, of which Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) [@ross2011reduction] is the classic form. In DAgger, an expert labels the states the learner itself visits and the policy retrains on the aggregate. @Sec-data-intervention-recovery develops DAgger, with its guarantee of a cost that grows linearly in the horizon (@eq-data-dagger-bound) and the recoverability constant $\DeviationDisadvantage$ on which that guarantee depends. The constant bounds how much a single deviation can raise the expert's remaining cost, so it is an assumption about the plant, not a property of the learner. On physical hardware, this theoretical recoverability depends directly on joint torque authority and contact friction limits.

On hardware, collecting those labels requires a recoverable rollout and an expert who has enough information to choose a correction. Because a camera log may support a path label while leaving contact force or joint torque ambiguous, live supervision supplies richer feedback, yet the machine continues moving during human reaction and control handoff. Consequently, intervention must begin within the available stopping margin, and the handoff must avoid discontinuous setpoints.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The bumpless transfer that keeps a human takeover from stepping the command is developed in @sec-intervention-bumpless-transfer.
:::

Expert availability also does not imply physical recoverability. The machine may lack enough actuator effort or frictional grip to return from a deviation. The simplified force balance $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix\GeneralizedAccelerations = \JointTorque + \ExternalContactTorque$ is Newton's second law written per joint: $\GeneralizedCoordinates$ denotes joint positions, $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix$ inertia, $\JointTorque$ actuator torque, and $\ExternalContactTorque$ the torque that contact forces exert about the joints; other forces are omitted here for clarity, and @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics develops the full equation. Actuator limits require $|\CommandedJointTorque_i| \le \JointTorqueLimit$ on every joint axis, while available friction bounds tangential force by $\|\TangentialContactShear\| \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce$, with normal force $\NormalContactForce$ and friction coefficient $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$. These constraints can leave no action that restores the task, and then $\DeviationDisadvantage$ is unbounded and DAgger's linear guarantee no longer applies. Interactive aggregation is therefore most useful where learner deviations can be contained, labeled, and repeated within the operator-time and hardware-exposure budget. The state space divides into three regions (@fig-06-compounding-error): the tube of demonstrated states where cloning trains, a band just outside it where an expert label on a learner-visited state still restores the task, and an unrecoverable region beyond, where actuator and friction limits leave no restoring action and every further label is vacuous. Interactive aggregation buys experience only in the middle band.

::: {#fig-06-compounding-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Drift out of the demonstrated states**: Behavioral cloning trains only inside the shaded tube the expert visited. Once the learner leaves it, each action is taken from an unfamiliar state and the error compounds. DAgger labels a learner-visited state outside the tube, which supplies recovery experience while a return is still possible. Past the red boundary, actuator and friction limits leave no action that restores the task, so no label can help. The sketch is schematic; its axes carry no units." fig-alt="Schematic state-space plot with task progress on the horizontal axis and deviation from the demonstrated path on the vertical axis. A shaded band surrounds a solid expert path. A dashed learner path leaves the band and continues upward into a red region at the top. At one point just outside the band, a marker labeled DAgger label has an arrow pointing back toward the band."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-06-compounding-error
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DRIFT OUT OF THE DEMONSTRATED STATES (STATE-SPACE SKETCH)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-06-compounding-error closes the DAgger and recoverability
# │          paragraphs of @sec-training-recovery-experience.
# │ Goal: Show where BC trains, where the learner goes, where DAgger labels,
# │       and where no label can help, in one picture.
# │ Show: demonstration tube around the expert path; learner drift leaving
# │       it; a DAgger label at a learner-visited state; the unrecoverable
# │       region bounded by actuator and friction limits.
# │ How: Schematic in dimensionless coordinates; no measured quantity is
# │      plotted, so the axes carry no ticks or units.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 3.8))
x = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 300)
expert = 0.10 * np.sin(2.2 * np.pi * x)  # demonstrated path (schematic)
tube = 0.14  # half-width of the demonstrated states
y_unrec = 0.78  # boundary of the unrecoverable region
x_leave = 0.30  # learner leaves the tube here
drift = 1.35 * np.clip(x - x_leave, 0.0, None) ** 1.6
learner = expert + 0.09 + drift  # learner path, offset then compounding

ax.axhspan(y_unrec, 1.0, color=COLORS["RedL"], lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axhline(y_unrec, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.4, zorder=1)
ax.text(0.02, 0.89, "Unrecoverable: no admissible action returns (torque, friction limits)", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontsize=9.5, va="center")
ax.fill_between(x, expert - tube, expert + tube, color=COLORS["GreenFill"], lw=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(x, expert, color=COLORS["GreenLine"], lw=2.0, zorder=3)
ax.text(0.97, -0.13, "Demonstrated states\n(BC trains here)", color=COLORS["GreenLine"], fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="top")
ax.text(0.03, -0.07, r"expert $\pi^*$", color=COLORS["GreenLine"], fontsize=9.5, va="top")
mask = learner <= y_unrec + 0.02
ax.plot(x[mask], learner[mask], color=COLORS["primary"], lw=2.0, ls="--", zorder=4)
i_end = np.argmax(~mask) - 1
ax.plot(x[i_end], learner[i_end], "o", color=COLORS["RedLine"], ms=6, zorder=5)
i_lab = np.searchsorted(x, 0.78)
ax.text(x[i_lab] - 0.02, learner[i_lab] + 0.02, r"learner $\pi_\theta$", color=COLORS["primary"], fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="bottom")

# DAgger: a learner-visited state just outside the tube gets an expert label.
i_d = np.searchsorted(x, 0.56)
xd, yd = x[i_d], learner[i_d]
ax.plot(xd, yd, "o", color=COLORS["primary"], ms=6, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "",
    xy=(xd + 0.05, expert[i_d + 15] + 0.08),
    xytext=(xd + 0.005, yd - 0.015),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["GreenLine"], lw=1.6),
    zorder=5,
)
ax.text(
    xd - 0.03,
    yd + 0.10,
    "DAgger: expert label\n" + r"$\pi^*(s)$ at a learner-visited $s$",
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    fontsize=9.5,
    ha="right",
    va="bottom",
)
ax.plot([xd - 0.028, xd - 0.004], [yd + 0.10, yd + 0.012], color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.8)

ax.set_xlim(0.0, 1.0)
ax.set_ylim(-0.30, 1.0)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Task progress")
ax.set_ylabel("Deviation from the demonstrated path")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

For the latch, these distinctions select a concrete next training step. The stipulated follow-up campaign in @sec-data-intervention-recovery supplies `latch-recovery-02`, a versioned archive of expert recovery from the positively displaced plate at the guarded approach. The recovery candidate `latch-bc-recovery-02` trains on the original nominal demonstrations and the stabilized, reviewed segment of each correction; the enforcer's blend and the operator's re-orientation after takeover stay masked. Learner commands that preceded takeover remain failure evidence unless an expert supplied replacement labels; they do not become imitation targets merely because the episode eventually succeeded. A multimodal chunk decoder can preserve a coherent back-off and re-seating sequence, while the additional demonstrations supply the recovery states that changing the decoder alone could not provide.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Causal intervention masking, which admits only reviewed recovery segments as imitation targets, is enforced in @sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility.
:::

The training decision is complete, but the improvement claim remains to be tested. Entire collection sessions are held out for nominal and recovery checks, so neighboring frames from one run do not appear on both sides of the split. Training diagnostics check whether the candidate represents the demonstrated correction; qualification must then test whether it completes the door task under the declared perturbation without regressing nominal behavior. The candidate carries that request to @sec-evaluation-recovery-update, including task completion, cycle time, proposer intervention, and protective outcomes as separate measures. This is a stipulated engineering branch, not a report of collected data or measured improvement. The negative displacement and faster approach remain unsupported, and even on the supported path, emitting setpoints one tick at a time leaves the arm vulnerable to the mode-boundary chattering of @sec-training-multimodality-breakdown unless the decoder predicts a multi-step action sequence in one pass.

### Action chunking and multi-step trajectory prediction {#sec-training-action-chunking}

Action chunking (definition \ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) suppresses both high-frequency actuator chattering and single-step mode oscillation by predicting an entire sequence of future actions simultaneously rather than re-querying the decoder at every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` control tick. Instead of regressing a single action $\ContinuousActionVector_{t}$ from current observation $\MultimodalObservation_{t}$, a chunking policy predicts a setpoint sequence $\ActionChunk_t \in \mathbb{R}^{\ActionChunkHorizon \times \ActionDimension}$ across a prediction horizon of $\ActionChunkHorizon$ future timesteps and $\ActionDimension$ action dimensions, which the execution path then interpolates into continuous motion and checks for feasibility. In supervised behavioral cloning, the policy minimizes a multi-step trajectory loss over demonstrated trajectories:
$$\ChunkImitationLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t^*) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \sum_{i=0}^{\ActionChunkHorizon-1} \ell_\HuberLossThreshold\left( \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t})_i - \ContinuousActionVector^*_{t+i} \right) \right],$$
where $\ActionChunk_t^* = [\ContinuousActionVector_t^*, \dots, \ContinuousActionVector_{t+\ActionChunkHorizon-1}^*]^\top$ represents the recorded demonstration chunk and $\Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t})_i$ is the $\ChunkStepIndex$-th predicted future setpoint. Actions are expressed in declared normalized coordinates. For a vector residual $\ActionResidualVector$, the chunk objective uses the componentwise sum $\ell_\HuberLossThreshold(\ActionResidualVector) = \sum_{j=1}^{\ActionDimension}\ell_\HuberLossThreshold(\NormalizedActionResidual_j)$, where $\NormalizedActionResidual_j$ is the matching component of $\ActionResidualVector$, with equal component weights; the scalar Huber penalty below acts on each normalized prediction error $\NormalizedActionResidual_j$, not on the reward of @sec-training-rl-primer:
$$\ell_\HuberLossThreshold(\NormalizedActionResidual) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \NormalizedActionResidual^2 & \text{for } |\NormalizedActionResidual| \le \HuberLossThreshold, \\ \HuberLossThreshold \left(|\NormalizedActionResidual| - \frac{1}{2} \HuberLossThreshold\right) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
(ACT [@zhao2023learning], the architecture of both latch policies, uses an $\ell_1$ reconstruction penalty in place of $\ell_\HuberLossThreshold$ and adds a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) term $\LatentKlWeight \KlDivergence(\LatentPosteriorDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \ActionChunk_t^*, \MultimodalObservation_{t}) \parallel \GaussianDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable))$ against a standard normal prior, which lets a latent variable absorb differences in style across demonstrations.)

Because teleoperated setpoints can contain outliers caused by tremor, tracking errors, or dropouts, squared loss gives a single large residual disproportionate influence over the fit. Huber loss[^fn-huber-loss-outliers] is quadratic for small residuals ($|\NormalizedActionResidual| \le \HuberLossThreshold$) and linear beyond them, so its gradient saturates at magnitude $\HuberLossThreshold$ and no single outlier can dominate the fit. Even so, the threshold acts on prediction residuals rather than on the velocity, acceleration, or jerk of the resulting trajectory, which means Huber loss alone establishes neither smooth motion nor actuator feasibility; those properties require explicit constraints and checks on the proposed chunk.

[^fn-huber-loss-outliers]: **Huber Loss**: @huber1964robust introduced it as an estimator of location that tolerates a small fraction of grossly wrong observations, quadratic near the center and linear in the tails, and showed that it minimizes the worst-case variance over such contaminated distributions. Teleoperation tremor and dropouts are exactly that contamination, and $\HuberLossThreshold$ sets, in the declared normalized action coordinates, where an error stops counting as noise and starts counting as a gross error. \index{Huber loss!robust estimation}

Predicting $\ActionChunkHorizon$ future actions at once creates opportunities for more coherent execution, provided training and runtime checks preserve them:

1. **Temporal and Dynamic Consistency**: Jointly predicting adjacent actions lets the model learn their relationships. The resulting sequence still requires checks for abrupt changes and actuator limits.
2. **Preserving Modal Commitment**: A chunk can represent one coherent choice, such as passing left of the column, across adjacent actions. Predicting a sequence does not itself ensure that the decoder selects a single valid mode.
3. **Receding-Horizon Replanning and Temporal Ensembling**: The deployed policy queries a fresh chunk every $\ChunkExecutionHorizon$ steps ($\ChunkExecutionHorizon < \ActionChunkHorizon$), permitting feedback correction before the prediction horizon ends. Blending overlapping predictions is optional and must preserve a coherent mode and feasible seam.

The modal commitment\index{Action chunking!mode commitment} that the chunk objective buys in training can be undone at execution. If stochastic sampling selects the left route at one query and the right route at the next, blending the overlapping chunks across the seam averages the two routes and resurrects the mode averaging\index{Temporal ensembling!mode averaging failure} that action chunking was chosen to eliminate [@black2025realtime].

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Temporal ensembling of overlapping chunks, and real-time chunking, which freezes the committed prefix and generates the rest of the next chunk to agree with it, are established in @sec-brain-action-chunking.
:::

Chunking changes how often the policy replans, but does not supply recovery states absent from the demonstrations. Executing $\ChunkExecutionHorizon$ actions between queries reduces the number of query boundaries to $\QueryBoundaryCount = \BehaviorCloningHorizon/\ChunkExecutionHorizon$ while leaving disturbances within each execution window to the lower-level feedback system. This count alone does not convert the imitation-learning cost bound $\mathcal{O}(\BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 \SingleStepImitationError)$ into a task-survival curve, the probability that an episode reaches the goal without entering an unrecoverable state, plotted against the horizon. ACT [@zhao2023learning] and receding-horizon diffusion [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] change temporal execution; DAgger [@ross2011reduction] changes the training distribution by obtaining labels on learner-visited states. These are separate ways to improve behavior, and their closed-loop benefits must be measured on the task. Neither the drift sketch of @fig-06-compounding-error nor the imitation-learning cost bound establishes a task-survival probability or ranks learning algorithms.

Increasing dataset size, model capacity, or tuning can reduce the one-step error rate on evaluated observations and therefore lower the chance of a first policy error during a fixed horizon. That improvement does not characterize what happens after an error. An external disturbance, uncalibrated payload, or voltage sag can also move the machine into weakly supported states without a policy disagreement. Recovery data, measured dynamics, and independent runtime limits determine whether either event remains within the physical envelope.

Drift off the demonstrated states raises no alarm of its own, so detecting it before physical contact cannot rely on the offline training loss. A feature-distance or uncertainty monitor can flag unfamiliar observations, but its threshold needs validation against missed detections and false alarms. For the latch, an independently measured plate position and approach condition provide a more direct check of the declared cells. A purely geometric monitor is weaker. One that accepts any state inside the convex hull of the demonstrated coordinates, a convex stand-in for the support hull of @sec-data-policy-coverage, still admits intermediate states that no demonstration visited, and nothing guarantees that those states are physically admissible or dynamically stable. Predicting an entire $\ActionChunkHorizon$-step chunk in a multimodal decoder solves the single-step averaging problem, but only if the hardware can finish evaluating that decoder before the next chunk is due.

### Decoder latency and proposal deadlines {#sec-training-decoder-costs}

Selecting a coherent route around an obstacle or into a latch does no good if the decoder finishes computing the trajectory after the actuator deadline has already passed. A decoder converts the model's representation into an action or action sequence; iterative decoders repeatedly refine a candidate before returning it. Their equations describe how a candidate is generated, while the execution decision depends on the wall-clock time those dependent model evaluations consume. The central comparison is between measured proposal latency and the deadline of the buffer that feeds the permission path.

The decoders that fix mode averaging buy that fix with time. A generative head escapes the regression mean by sampling one demonstrated route, but it reaches its sample through a chain of dependent refinements, and each refinement is another model evaluation that must finish before the next proposal is due (@fig-06-diffusion-denoising). The proposal then still has to cross from the application processor to the safety microcontroller's own buffer before the permission path can check it, so the decoder's time comes out of a budget it shares with transport and admission.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The placement of the multi-rate proposal and permission paths on the application processor and the safety microcontroller is developed in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

::: {#fig-06-diffusion-denoising fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Generative policy architectures and action chunk denoising**: (a) Sampling represents alternative demonstrated routes instead of their direct-regression mean. (b) Iterative refinement produces a candidate action chunk whose clearance and actuator feasibility still require checking. (c) On the machine's schedule, proposals renew every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` while setpoints play every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str`, and the bars compare the deployed ACT decoder with an illustrative diffusion head that leaves far less of each renewal period to spare. An admitted chunk crosses the black-channel link into the safety MCU's own double buffer and is checked on every permission tick before the drives act. Buffering alone guarantees neither freshness nor freedom from starvation." fig-alt="Three-panel diagram. Panel (a) contrasts direct regression, whose single mean arrow runs between two dashed demonstrated routes into an obstacle, with conditional diffusion, where a sample arrow from noise lands in one of two mode regions. Panel (b) shows three denoising stages, from a jagged noise trace at step N through a dashed coarse curve to a smooth action chunk at step 0 marked candidate only. Panel (c) is a timing strip over 125 milliseconds with rows for 40 millisecond ACT inference bars, dashed 48 millisecond diffusion bars with 2 milliseconds of slack, a 60 millisecond lease renewed at the next admission, setpoint ticks every 25 milliseconds, and a dense 1 kilohertz permission tick row. Beside it, a block chain runs from the application processor through a black-channel link to a safety MCU with active and filling buffers, then to the drives."}
![](images/svg/fig06_bespoke_diffusion_denoising_process.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The decoder families themselves, from binned and compressed action tokens to parallel heads and iterative action experts, are introduced in @sec-brain-learned-representations. What matters for training is their dependency structure. A diffusion policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] or a flow-matching expert [@lipman2022flow; @black2024pi0] refines a candidate chunk through evaluations that each consume the previous candidate, and an autoregressive vision-language-action policy [@kim2024openvla] generates its action tokens one after another, so in each case the dependent evaluations run in sequence. None of these constructions guarantees collision-free or actuator-feasible output, and the diffusion and flow-matching objectives are developed in @sec-appendix-ml-diffusion. Some post-training recipes remove the token sequence from the run-time path altogether by training a separate action expert (@sec-training-pretrain-post-train). For the latch decision, the relevant consequence is how many dependent evaluations yield adequate action quality, and the quantity that decides the execution arrangement is complete proposal latency, perception included, measured against the actual proposal deadline.

The number and dependency of decoder evaluations constrain proposal latency; the implementation and loaded hardware determine its measured value. The total wall-clock duration of a single policy inference cycle $\ProposerInferenceTime$ is the sum of perceptual feature extraction and iterative generative trajectory sampling:
$$\ProposerInferenceTime = \ObservationEncodingTime(\MultimodalObservation_{t}) + \sum_{k=1}^{\DecoderEvaluationCount} \DecoderPassTime\left(\NoisedActionChunk, \DiffusionStepIndex\right) \le \CompletionDeadline,$$ {#eq-training-decoder-latency}
where $\ObservationEncodingTime$ is the visual backbone and proprioceptive encoding latency, $\DecoderEvaluationCount$ is the number of dependent decoder evaluations (denoising or ODE solver steps), $\DecoderPassTime$ is the latency of one forward pass of the action head (one denoising or solver step, not the whole-model evaluation time $\ProposerInferenceTime$ of @eq-brain-eval-latency), $\NoisedActionChunk$ is the candidate chunk that the $\DiffusionStepIndex$-th evaluation refines, and $\CompletionDeadline$ is the real-time execution deadline.

The encoder runs once per proposal, whereas each dependent decoder evaluation adds work. @Sec-brain-action-chunking prices that work for each decoder family on the machine's processor, where re-reading a large action head on every evaluation can dominate it. Training decides the two quantities those prices depend on, the head and its evaluation count $\DecoderEvaluationCount$, so the question here is whether a head chosen for its multimodal fit also meets the latch's deadlines.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-decoder-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DECODER BUDGET: THE DEPLOYED ACT DECODER VERSUS A 16-STEP DIFFUSION HEAD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-training-decoder-costs and the latch policy manifest.
# │ Goal: Price an iterative diffusion head that could replace the one-pass
# │       ACT decoder of latch-bc-01 against the machine's setpoint step,
# │       renewal period, and the lease rule's jitter allowance.
# │ Show: 48 ms stipulated DDIM latency and 2.5 ms per evaluation; 18 ms
# │       for four flow evaluations; 2 ms of renewal slack against ACT's
# │       10 ms; a 5 ms stretch carries the diffusion head 3 ms past its
# │       renewal. The weight-streaming floor is priced in
# │       @sec-brain-action-chunking, not here (coherence P1-4).
# │ How: t_eval = (t_infer - t_enc) / K; deployed decoder and periods from
# │      RM (2026-09-28, M5).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class DecoderBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    act_params = RM.chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet (ACT, the deployed chunk policy)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (setpoints per chunk)
    t_act = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    t_step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (setpoint step, synchronous deadline)
    t_renew = RM.chunk_period  # category: derived (renewal period, asynchronous deadline)
    k_ddim = 16  # category: illustrative (DDIM denoising steps)
    k_flow = 4  # category: illustrative (flow-matching evaluations)
    t_enc = 8 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (visual encoding, once per proposal)
    t_ddim = 48 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (stipulated total DDIM inference)
    t_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-lease-sizing)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_eval = ((t_ddim - t_enc) / k_ddim).to(millisecond)
    t_flow = (t_enc + k_flow * t_eval).to(millisecond)
    slack_act = (t_renew - t_act).to(millisecond)
    slack_ddim = (t_renew - t_ddim).to(millisecond)
    ddim_stretch_over = (t_ddim + t_jitter - t_renew).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_eval.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, f"per-evaluation time {t_eval}")
    check(abs(t_flow.magnitude - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"flow latency {t_flow}")
    check(t_ddim > t_step, "DDIM must overrun the synchronous setpoint deadline")
    check(t_flow < t_step, "four flow evaluations must fit the synchronous setpoint deadline")
    check(t_act < t_ddim < t_renew, "both decoders must fit the renewal period, ACT with more slack")
    check(abs(slack_act.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9 and abs(slack_ddim.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "renewal slack")
    check(t_act + t_jitter < t_renew, "a jitter-sized stretch must leave ACT inside its renewal period")
    check(abs(ddim_stretch_over.magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, f"diffusion overrun under stretch {ddim_stretch_over}")
    # margin_generative_inference_deadlines_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 40, 18, 48, 25, and 50 ms.
    check((t_act.magnitude, t_ddim.magnitude, t_step.magnitude) == (40.0, 48.0, 25.0), "envelope fig-alt values")
    check(abs(t_renew.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"renewal period {t_renew}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    act_params_str = fmt_params(act_params, precision=0)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    k_ddim_str = fmt_int(k_ddim)
    k_flow_str = fmt_int(k_flow)
    t_enc_str = fmt_latency(t_enc, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ddim_str = fmt_latency(t_ddim, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_eval_str = fmt_latency(t_eval, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_flow_str = fmt_latency(t_flow, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    slack_act_str = fmt_latency(slack_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    slack_ddim_str = fmt_latency(slack_ddim, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```
