Without explicit cooling intervals scheduled between training episodes, this continuous Joule heating\index{Joule heating!actuator thermal limits} can push motor windings to their thermal derating threshold within minutes.

Demonstrating improved performance on a specific contact fixture does not prove that the overall manipulation task remains sound. An optimization step yielding a parameter update $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ produces an entirely distinct model checkpoint. Empirical evaluations gathered on the prior policy $\ModelParameters_0$ remain historical observations of $\ModelParameters_0$ alone; they do not substantiate safety claims for the updated weights\index{Statistical verification!collapse under fine-tuning}. Gradient updates that successfully minimize contact forces on the strike plate can inadvertently distort free-space approach trajectories or degrade emergency stopping profiles in operational regions absent from the fine-tuning rollouts\index{Catastrophic forgetting!in physical fine-tuning}. Because physical trials consume valuable robot runtime and cause mechanical wear, requalification protocols must be strictly prioritized to verify both the targeted contact improvement and the baseline capabilities the update could destabilize.

Each updated checkpoint must carry its own explicit configuration manifest and regression evidence before deployment. Moreover, while optimization progresses on physical hardware, the safety permission path must actively evaluate every candidate action proposed by intermediate policies. Restricting where learned corrections may act keeps unconstrained weight updates from corrupting verified behaviors.

### Residual policy architectures and bounded authority {#sec-training-residual-architectures}

Residual architectures prevent unconstrained weight updates from emitting nonzero drift commands in free space by freezing the base policy weights and multiplying the learned additive correction by an independently enforced binary gate:
$$\NominalControlCommand(\DecisionProcessState) = \pi_{\text{base}}(\DecisionProcessState) + \ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\,\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState),$$ {#eq-training-gated-residual}
where $\pi_{\text{base}}$ is the frozen base controller, $\FiniteChange\Policy$ is a learned contact correction trained via reinforcement learning on the physical machine against the latch reward of @eq-training-latch-reward [@silver2018residual; @johannink2019residual], and $\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\in\{0,1\}$ is an independently evaluated deterministic gate that equals one only within the certified contact envelope.

Both the base policy and the composite controller require explicit verification, because freezing an unverified base policy such as `latch-sim-02` does not make it qualified for deployment. Instead, the role of the gate $\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)$ is structural: it forces the residual correction to evaluate *identically to zero* in free space and across all non-contact states, where an absence of reward gradients during training would still allow a function approximator to output nonzero values on out-of-distribution inputs. Before any command reaches physical actuators, the permission path verifies the validity of the current state estimate (the machine's fused estimate of its own configuration, developed in @sec-memory) and audits the proposed composite action.

Relying on a soft training loss, such as an action-norm penalty $\|\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState)\|^2$, merely biases the optimizer toward modest corrections during nominal rollouts; it offers no deterministic runtime guarantee. In contrast, the independent gate explicitly revokes residual authority whenever the robot operates outside designated regimes. Even with an architectural gate, the verification suite must evaluate transient switching behaviors at gate boundaries, state-estimation latency, execution timing jitter, and joint torque limits under the combined controller.

Imposing an output magnitude ceiling, $\|\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState)\|\le\ResidualCorrectionCeiling$, restricts only one dimension of authority. A production permission path must also enforce slew-rate limits on the correction delta, prevent joint limit violations, verify multi-axis dynamic feasibility, and invoke the qualified fallback when active execution loses valid state, evidence, or lease. A late replacement proposal does not revoke a still-valid active prefix; that prefix may continue only within its own validity conditions. Furthermore, the authorized residual envelope must lie strictly within the verified stability margin of the *combined* closed-loop system across its intended operating envelope; checking an isolated torque limit against an idealized, single-axis specification is never sufficient. For the latch fixture, for instance, the architecture activates residual corrections exclusively during confirmed physical contact, enforces a hard zero via the gate throughout the free-space approach, and clamps joint torque slew rates. Following each optimization step on hardware, an automated regression suite must re-verify free-space trajectory tracking, contact engagement forces, emergency stopping, thermal duty cycles, and drivetrain shock profiles before granting operational authority to the new checkpoint. An improperly verified residual, even when clipped in magnitude, can still induce limit-cycle oscillations or drive the actuator gearboxes into saturation. Freezing the base policy and gating an additive residual is the most localized way to refine a policy with rewards; other post-training regimes modify the decoder's input noise or update every weight in the network, widening the regression scope accordingly.

### Reinforcement learning after pretraining {#sec-training-rl-post-training}

The gated residual is one member of a broader family of post-training regimes. Every method that refines a pretrained policy using environmental rewards must specify which parameters are allowed to change—because updating shared weights to double throughput on one fixture can silently degrade baseline behaviors elsewhere—and that choice determines how much regression evidence is required to re-qualify the resulting checkpoint. Modern robotic systems use four primary post-training strategies (@tbl-06-state-of-practice):

- **Residual control** freezes the base policy weights and learns an additive correction term, exactly as demonstrated by `latch-res-03`. This strategy has been successfully deployed to refine frozen chunked imitation policies for high-precision assembly, training the residual policy via PPO in simulation [@ankile2025residual]. Residual architectures are straightforward to bound because independent hardware permission logic can directly gate, saturate, and rate-limit the additive output.
- **Noise-space steering** freezes every parameter of an underlying diffusion or flow-matching policy, training an auxiliary policy only to predict the initial latent noise vector supplied to the reverse diffusion trajectory. Every proposed trajectory still passes through the frozen generative decoder, so steering is restricted to outputs that decoder can generate. This restriction does not establish that those outputs lie within demonstrated support or satisfy physical limits. Furthermore, the optimizer requires only black-box sampling access to the base policy [@wagenmaker2025dsrl]. Here, the support of the base distribution constrains the proposed behaviors; the independent permission path must still determine whether those proposals may execute.
- **Advantage-conditioned post-training** updates all network weights using supervised learning conditioned on advantage estimates. A learned critic evaluates the advantage of candidate actions across human demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and real-time human interventions; the policy is then trained on this mixed corpus conditioned on target advantage and queried for high-advantage actions at run time. Applied to generalist robot manipulation models, this approach more than doubled throughput and halved failure rates on the reported physical manipulation tasks [@physicalintelligence2025recap]. However, because gradient updates modify every weight in the network, all nominal behaviors remain subject to drift.
- **Policy-gradient fine-tuning in simulation** applies reinforcement learning techniques (@sec-training-parallel-simulation) to update the weights of a pretrained vision-language-action policy using sparse or binary success rewards in massively parallel simulation [@li2025simplevlarl]. Like advantage conditioning, this paradigm modifies all network parameters; in addition, it inherits every physical approximation and contact-solver idealization present in the underlying simulation environment.

Regression scope follows where the composite output can change and which execution assumptions the update affects. An independently enforced residual gate localizes the changed output, but regression still covers its active region, boundary transitions, combined closed-loop behavior, and timing and resource effects. Noise-space steering can change sampling throughout the base domain despite frozen decoder weights, so every affected operating mode requires regression unless a separate gate establishes a narrower scope. Full-weight updates can also alter behaviors across the entire operational envelope. A newly fine-tuned full-weight model demands complete end-to-end regression testing across all previously validated operational modes, and the system's `adaptation_wear_log` must document every modified parameter group. Whether adaptation rollouts accumulate physical machine wear on hardware or incur modeling dependencies in simulation, each rollout must be recorded in the policy manifest. No model can legitimately claim expanded operational authority without concrete validation data recorded in the system audit log.

| Regime                                | Named Systems                                                                                                                    | Mechanism Taught in This Chapter                                                  | What the Policy Manifest Must Record                                                     |
|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Pretrain, then post-train**         | Octo [@octo_2023]; OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla]; $\pi_0$ [@black2024pi0]; $\pi_{0.5}$ [@black2025pi05]; GR00T N1 [@bjorck2025gr00t] | Pretraining on pooled multi-robot data, then supervised post-training on the task | Base weight digest; pretraining mixture as a known unknown; action-space mapping         |
| **Post-training recipe**              | OpenVLA-OFT [@kim2025openvlaoft]                                                                                                 | Action chunking with parallel decoding and an $\ell_1$ regression head            | Decoder latency of the new head against the proposal deadline                            |
| **RL post-training on the machine**   | $\pi^*_{0.6}$ with RECAP [@physicalintelligence2025recap]                                                                        | Advantage-conditioned updates from autonomous experience and corrections          | Full-weight change; corrections as authority-record entries; regression over base domain |
| **RL post-training in simulation**    | SimpleVLA-RL [@li2025simplevlarl]                                                                                                | Policy gradient with a binary success reward in a parallel simulator              | Simulator provenance and omission log                                                    |
| **Frozen-policy steering**            | DSRL [@wagenmaker2025dsrl]                                                                                                       | Reinforcement learning over the decoder's input noise, base weights unchanged     | Base digest unchanged; steering policy digest                                            |
| **Residual RL**                       | ResiP [@ankile2025residual]                                                                                                      | Residual trained by PPO on a frozen chunked imitation policy                      | Gate, magnitude, and slew limits; regression where the residual acts                     |
| **Real-world RL from demonstrations** | HIL-SERL [@luo2025hilserl]                                                                                                       | Demonstrations, interventions, and a learned success reward with off-policy reuse | Success classifier as a learned sensor; interventions as authority-record entries        |
| **GPU-parallel simulation**           | Isaac Lab [@mittal2025isaaclab]; MuJoCo Playground [@zakka2025playground]                                                        | Batched, accelerator-resident physics feeding on-policy learning                  | Solver build and contact settings; throughput stated with its scene                      |
| **World models**                      | DreamerV3 [@hafner2025dreamerv3]; V-JEPA 2 [@assran2025vjepa2]; Cosmos [@nvidia2025cosmos]                                       | Learned dynamics for imagined rollouts, planning, synthetic data, and evaluation  | Model weight digest and training data; generated experience unqualified                  |

: **State of practice in robot policy training, as of 2026**: Named systems that instantiate the mechanisms this chapter teaches, dated by their cited publications. The systems will be superseded; the mechanism and manifest columns are the durable part of the table. {#tbl-06-state-of-practice tbl-colwidths="[18,30,26,26]"}

Bounded residual authority restricts the influence of an exploratory policy during execution, but it cannot alone prevent mechanical damage or eliminate latent vulnerabilities introduced during earlier training phases. Every stage of policy synthesis, from demonstration ingestion and simulation contact mechanics to residual adaptation, leaves a distinct behavioral signature on closed-loop execution. When an embodied machine develops high-frequency chattering, thermal derating, or semantic drift, systems engineers can trace that failure behavior directly back to the training assumptions, solver compromises, and architectural trade-offs that created it.

## Training Failure Modes and Permission-Path Interceptors {#sec-training-failure-modes}

A physical failure in a learned policy is rarely arbitrary. When an end-effector collides with a strike plate, that command reflects optimization over a specific dataset, loss formulation, and simulator dynamics, and the two failures that opened the chapter can now be traced back to theirs. The assumptions baked into that optimization leave a structural footprint on policy behavior, one that engineers can trace and mitigate before hardware ever runs. The **policy vulnerability inference chain**\index{Policy vulnerability inference chain}\index{Vulnerability analysis!training regimes} makes this causal trace explicit across five links: ($\text{Exposure} \to \text{Dependency} \to \text{Violated Assumption} \to \text{Observable Signature} \to \text{Permission-Path Interceptor}$). Training exposure establishes a learned dependency; an unmodeled deployment condition violates that dependency; the violation produces a measurable signature in the commands or physical plant telemetry; and that signature names the specific runtime interceptor that the execution permission path requires. Reading the three latch checkpoints back through this chain shows how distinct optimization regimes produce different failure modes.

For `latch-bc-01`, behavioral cloning relies on the teleoperated openings. These demonstrations only support nominal plate alignment during the guarded approach; the data-collection campaign never demonstrated a displaced or misaligned plate. A sagging door frame directly violates that geometric dependency. The resulting failure signature is compounding covariate shift\index{Covariate shift!in behavioral cloning}. Because behavioral cloning optimizes an open-loop supervised objective over expert trajectories, small drift errors compound at each control step. Individual motion proposals often remain physically plausible right up until the gripper mechanically binds against the frame. To prevent mechanical damage, a support monitor must evaluate runtime observations against the empirically supported demonstration cells and revoke policy authority outside them. Predeployment qualification follows directly from the known coverage gap that the scenario table of @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability-geometry recorded: bench trials with deliberately displaced plates must confirm that the support monitor trips reliably before the mechanism binds.

For `latch-sim-02`, training inside a physics simulator instills strong dependencies on idealized contact dynamics and negligible actuation lag. A physical steel plate violates both assumptions, generating sharp contact forces and unmodeled transport delays that produce the overforce transients quantified in @sec-training-contact-exploit. Paired contact probes expose this dynamical mismatch before hardware deployment. If the physical contact deadline leaves insufficient time for closed-loop deceleration, a reactive force tripwire arrives too late. Detecting a force excursion confirms that an impact occurred, but actuator inertia and mechanical compliance will continue driving the mechanism into the plate before the brakes can arrest motion. The interceptor is therefore the pre-contact stopping envelope of @sec-training-contact-exploit, which guarantees a full stop at the standoff before the plate and hands engagement beyond it to the separately qualified guarded contact mode.

For `latch-res-03`, adaptation concentrates real-robot experience on the contact states of a single hardware rig. Localized fine-tuning targets tight-tolerance contact dynamics on that specific fixture, but it does not qualify the frozen base across the rest of the operational state space. Unlike full-weight fine-tuning, which can introduce catastrophic forgetting\index{Catastrophic forgetting!fine-tuning regression}, this gated residual retains the base weights and holds corrections at zero in free space; its primary regression risks arise from contact corrections and gate-boundary transitions. Before updated weights receive operational authority, they must clear a frozen regression suite that evaluates both nominal latch engagement and free-space flight. In addition, an architectural residual gate must hold corrections at zero outside the designated contact phase, preventing fine-tuned offsets from destabilizing the free-space approach. Physical exploration during real-machine tuning (@sec-training-real-machine-tuning) also imposes mechanical shock and motor winding heat; the runtime supervisor must monitor these thermal and structural thresholds continuously to ensure that task reward improvements do not mask hardware degradation.

Subsequent training stages do not automatically heal the unresolved dependencies of earlier stages. In the simulation-and-residual lineage (`latch-sim-02` through `latch-res-03`), simulation artifacts persist until physical hardware evidence explicitly closes them. Conversely, the recovery-imitation branch adopts an alternative architectural path. The checkpoint `latch-bc-recovery-02` incorporates targeted, human-guided recovery demonstrations for a named displaced-plate condition, expanding the operational envelope without relying on an uncalibrated simulator. Its remaining engineering uncertainties, chiefly closed-loop trajectory stability and potential regression on nominal openings, are made explicit through targeted qualification requests.

Ultimately, each inference chain connects a specific training assumption to an empirical test and an active execution limit. The policy manifest preserves these connections alongside the checkpoint's source data, simulator configuration, optimization objective, and architectural constraints. By maintaining this end-to-end traceability, verification suites can systematically evaluate candidate policies against the exact physical vulnerabilities created by their training history.

## The Policy Manifest {#sec-training-policy-manifest}

Handing a candidate checkpoint to an evaluation team with only its weight file and a training curve hides whether its behavior on a displaced plate comes from human recovery demonstrations, uncalibrated simulator rollouts, or pure network extrapolation. The candidate selection must distinguish nominal behavior supported by demonstrations, newly taught recovery, and contact behavior that still depends on unverified simulation. The failure chains of @sec-training-failure-modes make that distinction concrete for each checkpoint; the record accompanying the candidate into evaluation preserves the reasoning, including the assumptions that remain open.

The **policy manifest**\index{Policy manifest!definition} records how a checkpoint was produced: its training stages, the data support it inherits from the provenance records, its simulator versions and the **omission log**\index{Policy manifest!omission log} of mechanisms they leave out and mismatches paired probes have not closed, the wear incurred during adaptation, and the operating domain it declares (@tbl-06-training-schema). These fields state what evaluation must test and what runtime enforcement must accommodate. The runtime safety supervisor can check the manifest against its validated configuration before enabling a checkpoint. A declared boundary does not automatically generate a reliable detector or a safe clamp; those mechanisms require their own engineering and evidence.

The manifest separates optimization results from the conditions the policy may be asked to operate in\index{Operational design domain!training boundaries}. The **declared ODD** is the part of the ODD from @sec-data-policy-coverage that the policy manifest claims: the supported cells of the data join, minus every state the omission log excludes. High training reward or low offline loss does not show that the policy is safe outside it, so the declared ODD is computed from the join and the log, never from the training curve, and a convergent metric cannot stand in for clearance over regimes nobody characterized.

The separate `latch-bc-recovery-02` manifest consumes the original provenance and the stipulated `latch-recovery-02` archive, adding the positively displaced-plate cell at the guarded approach to the candidate domain with the expert recovery labels and held-out sessions identified by digest. Its qualification request asks whether the updated policy completes that recovery and preserves nominal service under the same physical limits, while the original archive remains unchanged and negative displacement and the fast approach remain excluded. Current provenance bounds the evidence already available, whereas collecting and qualifying new experience expands the machine's useful competence.

| Record Schema Field             | Recorded Quantities and Artifacts                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Provenance & Immutability Guarantee                                                            | Downstream Verifier & Usage                                                                                                    |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **`regime_sequence`**           | Array of optimization stages ($\text{BC} \to \text{SimRL} \to \text{Distill} \to \text{Residual}$), loss formulas, teacher privileged state dimensions ($\ContactWrench, \SimulationParameterVector$), student observation history length $\ObservationHistoryLength$, reward weights, and stopping criteria hashes       | Git commit SHA, PyTorch/JAX checkpoint UUIDs, parameter hash $\text{hash}(\ModelParameters_k)$ | Tracing which regime introduced latent failure modes or high-gain chatter                                                      |
| **`base_checkpoint`**           | Weight digest of any pretrained checkpoint the policy started from, its source, the action-space mapping applied, and the layers post-training changed; the pretraining mixture recorded as a known unknown when it cannot be cited by digest                                                                             | Base weight digest; never counted as data support                                              | Scopes forgetting regression tests; confirms that no supported cell is attributed to pretraining                               |
| **`policy_inference_contract`** | Model architecture class, parameter count, checkpoint weights hash $\text{hash}(\ModelParameters)$, chunk prediction horizon $\ActionChunkHorizon$, execution horizon $\ExecutionHorizon$, decoder evaluations $\DecoderEvaluationCount$, inference deadline $\ChunkRenewalPeriod$, and chunk lease $\ChunkLease$         | Cryptographic checkpoint hash $\text{hash}(\ModelParameters)$, compiled engine digest          | Parameterizes the runtime proposal buffer (@sec-brain-action-chunking) and real-time lease monitor (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing) |
| **`data_support`**              | Digests of the consumed provenance records and of the scenario table they were measured against; the `supported_cells` and `known_absences` of their occupancy join                                                                                                                                                       | Cites each provenance record by digest; no dataset field is copied                             | Upper bound on the declared ODD; parameterizes out-of-distribution support monitors                                            |
| **`negative_event_registry`**   | Authority-record entries (@sec-data-intervention-recovery) from training and adaptation rollouts                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Cites each authority-record entry by digest; its pre-trigger trace is not copied               | Isolating physical failure boundaries and preventing corrupted drift rollouts from training                                    |
| **`simulation_provenance`**     | Physics engine build, integrator method, timestep $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, contact solver penalty parameters, and domain randomization ranges $\ParameterRandomizationRanges(\SimulationParameterSet)$ with their source (measurement or curriculum); for a learned world model, its weight digest and training data | Physics engine binary hash, robot model asset tree hash (URDF/MJCF)                            | Reproducing the training physics and auditing paired-trace budgets                                                             |
| **`omission_log`**              | Mechanisms each simulator leaves out (backlash, compliance, transport lag) and the residual mismatches paired probes did not close, with the states each one affects                                                                                                                                                      | Bound to the simulator build it describes; an entry closes only on paired-trace evidence       | Removes the states it affects from the declared ODD; carried into evaluation's coverage gaps and the fault list                |
| **`adaptation_wear_log`**       | Serialized hardware IDs, contact shock counts, motor current RMS thermal logs, modified layer indices, and regression suite hash                                                                                                                                                                                          | Calibration certificate hashes, hardware lifetime fatigue logs                                 | Re-opening formal qualification cases and preventing silent regression of nominal capabilities                                 |
| **`declared_odd_boundary`**     | Declared ODD: the supported cells minus the states the omission log excludes (for the latch policy, the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach speed)                                                                                                                                                               | Never exceeds the supported cells of `data_support`                                            | Bounds the target ODD that evaluation may sample and the region in which the permission path admits policy proposals           |

: **Policy manifest schema**: Fields the policy manifest adds to the provenance records it consumes, recording policy synthesis stages, any pretrained base checkpoint, inference execution parameters, data support by digest, physics engine specifications and their omission log, hardware fine-tuning wear, and the declared ODD. {#tbl-06-training-schema tbl-colwidths="[20,18,22,40]"}

For the original latch campaign and its simulation-residual lineage, a compact manifest links the fields into one decision:

- `regime_sequence`: demonstration checkpoint `latch-bc-01` → `latch-sim-02`, a student initialized from `latch-bc-01` and distilled from a simulator teacher trained by reinforcement learning on privileged state (privileged contact wrenches $\ContactWrench$ distilled into an 8-step observation-history buffer) → gated residual candidate `latch-res-03`; retain each checkpoint hash, loss or reward specification, and stop rule.
- `base_checkpoint`: no pretrained robot policy underlies the latch checkpoints, which descend from `latch-bc-01` as `regime_sequence` records; any pretrained image encoder they use belongs here by digest. A candidate post-trained from the machine's intent model would record that model's weight digest, its pretraining mixture as a known unknown, and its action-space mapping, and would inherit the same declared ODD (@sec-training-pretrain-post-train).
- `policy_inference_contract`: specify checkpoint weights hash $\text{hash}(\ModelParameters)$, the machine's `{python} DecoderBudget.act_params_str`-parameter ACT architecture with one decoder pass per chunk, chunk prediction horizon $\ActionChunkHorizon =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str`, and the `{python} DecoderBudget.t_act_str` p99 inference target; record the selected execution prefix separately from the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` proposal-renewal deadline and the selected chunk lease. Each renewed prefix requires valid evidence and a feasible continuation or fallback; the prediction horizon is not the active lease.
- `data_support`: cite the latch campaign's provenance records and its scenario table by digest; their join supports the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, and lists the displaced plate and the faster approach, whose cells hold no demonstrations, as known absences with no recovery label.
- `simulation_provenance`: record the actual solver build and contact parameters.
- `omission_log`: the example simulator models strike-plate contact with a penalty spring far softer than the plate and omits actuator transport lag, so the contact states those two departures govern are unverified for the checkpoints trained in simulation.
- `negative_event_registry`:\index{Negative event registry}\index{Pre-trigger ring buffer} cite by digest the authority-record entry, with its pre-trigger ring-buffer trace, for every fixture-shoulder strike, operator veto, or permission-path clamp with its event classification, without treating rejected learner commands as expert targets, and mark episodes an operator truncated so that an update does not score an aborted command as a success.
- `adaptation_wear_log`:\index{Adaptation wear log} associate `latch-res-03` with the specific rig, above-threshold samples and separately identified contact events, motor-current history, modified residual weights, and free-space regression result.
- `declared_odd_boundary`: the supported cells minus the states the omission log excludes, here the nominal plate at the guarded approach of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded_str`. The contact states governed by the two omissions stay outside the declared ODD for every simulation-refined checkpoint, `latch-sim-02` and `latch-res-03` alike, until paired probes close them. The displaced plate and the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_fast_str` approach lie outside it, and the fast approach would stay outside even with demonstrations, because its contact deadline (@sec-training-contact-exploit) leaves almost nothing beyond the contact-loop response; there the permission path must impose the guarded approach or refuse policy authority.

A qualification review would withhold operational authority from `latch-res-03` until paired contact probes quantify the contact-stiffness error and the omitted lag, and the combined controller passes contact, free-space, stopping, and wear-budget tests. With only the original campaign, the same rule leaves `latch-bc-01` as the checkpoint evaluation may sample, provided the support monitor of its chain refuses policy authority off the nominal plate (@sec-training-failure-modes). Trained without a simulator, it carries no omission-log exclusions, so its declared ODD keeps the door's contact states at the nominal plate and the guarded approach. The manifest records that decision and its evidence rather than converting a training score into permission.

The manifest references the collector, plant, calibration, and action taps through the provenance record of @sec-data-schema. The cited digests preserve which data and scenario table produced the checkpoint; later changes require a new record rather than silently updating its lineage. Simulator provenance similarly fixes the solver and timestep[^fn-contact-sim-timestep] used during optimization. Its separate omission log carries unresolved discrepancies from @sec-training-sim-to-real-gap into evaluation's coverage gaps and fault-injection tests.

[^fn-contact-sim-timestep]: **Penalty-Contact Timestep**: The contact timescale scales as $\sqrt{\EffectiveImpactMass/\EffectiveSeriesStiffness}$. For the latch's `{python} LatchContactExploit.m_task_str` moving mass it is about `{python} LatchContactExploit.t_contact_sim_str` against the soft penalty spring and `{python} LatchContactExploit.t_contact_plate_str` against the real plate, so a timestep sized to resolve the simulated contact is about `{python} LatchContactExploit.t_contact_ratio_mult_str` too coarse once the spring is stiffened to match the plate. The integrator, damping, and solver tolerances set the final step, which is refined until contact onset, peak force, and impulse converge. \index{Simulation!timestep bounds}

Downstream engineering teams consume the manifest throughout the design, evaluation, and release lifecycle. The evaluation record of @sec-evaluation-logs consumes it directly. Its target ODD is sampled from inside the declared ODD, and its catalog of coverage gaps inherits the known absences and the omission log, so evaluation suites probe the specific failure modes each training regime predicts. Targeted exploratory tests outside the candidate domain can also identify gaps, but they do not establish an operational claim there without new support and qualification. The permission path takes the declared ODD as the outer limit of the region in which it admits policy proposals, and uses the recorded support to parameterize out-of-distribution detectors. Verification and the safety case draw on the manifest to establish the provenance of every parameter update and to confirm that each omission is bounded by an independent physical interlock.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The omission log becomes one of the upstream records from which fault records are compiled for release, developed in @sec-verification-fault-manifest.
:::

::: {#chk-training-provenance-record .callout-checkpoint title="Policy manifests and declared ODDs"}

Before releasing a trained policy checkpoint to physical verification, confirm the following relationships between the policy manifest, its omission log, and the declared ODD:

- [ ] **Complete the latch record**: A fixture-shoulder strike appears after `latch-res-03` was trained with a soft penalty contact and no actuator lag. Which omitted mechanism belongs in `omission_log`, and which paired probe and admission decision must the manifest record?
- [ ] **Confining the declared ODD**: Suppose demonstrations were collected at the fast approach and every omission-log entry were closed by paired probes. Why would the latch policy's declared ODD still exclude the fast approach, which timing comparison decides it, and what must the permission path impose on a proposal that arrives at that speed?
- [ ] **Negative event logging**: Why does the manifest keep the pre-trigger trace of an operator veto or fixture strike as labeled failure evidence rather than as an imitation target?
- [ ] **Declared operational boundaries**: `latch-bc-01` proposes to open the door while the strike plate sits displaced from its nominal mount. How does the permission path use the `data_support` field to classify that state as ungrounded extrapolation rather than demonstrated competence, and why does a confident policy output not change the classification?
:::

The manifest turns a training history into a claim with stated limits. The original record sends `latch-bc-01` to evaluation and keeps `latch-res-03` out of service until paired probes and regression tests close its gaps. The stipulated recovery record sends `latch-bc-recovery-02` with a wider, explicitly testable candidate claim. The common ways that decision goes wrong all let a training score stand in for that evidence.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-training-fallacies-pitfalls}

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-fallacy-scenarios
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FALLACY SCENARIOS: CHATTER, FINE-TUNING, AND RANDOMIZATION RANGES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-training-fallacies-pitfalls (simulation-RL chatter, online
# │          fine-tuning, and widened domain randomization fallacies).
# │ Goal: Keep each fallacy's scenario values out of hand-typed prose.
# │ Show: the chatter frequency, the fine-tuning step count, the mass
# │       randomization spread, and the friction-coefficient interval.
# │ How: No arithmetic; every value is an illustrative scenario input. The
# │      action-filter cutoff is shared with @tbl-06-reality-gap.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import hertz

class FallacyScenarios:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    f_chatter = 65.0 * hertz  # category: illustrative (torque chatter of the sim-RL gasket policy)
    n_finetune_steps = 5000  # category: illustrative (online fine-tuning steps)
    mass_spread = 0.50  # category: illustrative (± link-mass randomization, fraction)
    mu_lo = 0.05  # category: illustrative (friction-coefficient range, low end)
    mu_hi = 1.5  # category: illustrative (friction-coefficient range, high end)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    f_cutoff = RealityGapTable.f_cutoff  # the countermeasure's action-filter cutoff

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(f_cutoff < f_chatter, "the action filter must cut below the chatter frequency")
    check(mu_lo < mu_hi, "the friction interval must be ordered")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_chatter_str = fmt_frequency(f_chatter, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    n_finetune_steps_str = fmt_count(n_finetune_steps)
    mass_spread_pct_str = fmt_percent(mass_spread, precision=0, style="prose")
    mu_lo_str = fmt(mu_lo, precision=2)
    mu_hi_str = fmt(mu_hi, precision=1)
    f_cutoff_str = fmt_frequency(f_cutoff, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

Minimizing loss on an offline demonstration split or maximizing cumulative return in simulation measures compliance with training assumptions rather than physical competence on hardware. When an objective rewards behavior that exploits a curated demonstration distribution or a simulator approximation, the ranking of candidates established in training can invert on deployment\index{Deployment!policy ranking inversion}: the candidate that scored highest in simulation finishes lowest on hardware, through unsupported state drift, contact-force spikes past the structural limit, or torque oscillations that grow into resonant chatter (@fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion). Virtual environments forgive maneuvers that physical hardware penalizes with tripwires, resonance, or thermal overload, so the causal assumptions connecting a training metric to physical execution have to be tested before a policy receives actuator authority.

::: {#fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative policy ranking inversion**: (a) A constructed slope graph shows how a candidate favored by a simulated score can lose its advantage under physical evaluation. (b) Possible causes include unsupported recovery states, contact mismatch, and actuator chatter. The rankings are a teaching example, not measured results for the latch checkpoints." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel (a) is a slope graph between a simulated-score axis and a hardware-result axis: a red line runs from the exploiting policy high on the simulated score down to low on hardware, and a dark line runs from the robust policy low on the simulated score up to high on hardware, so the lines cross. Panel (b) stacks three small traces: a state trace that drifts out of a shaded band of demonstrated states, a contact force whose red spike rises above a dashed force limit, and an oscillation that grows into large chatter where the actuation frequency matches the resonance frequency."}
![](images/svg/fig06_policy_ranking_inversion.svg){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Sanitizing recovery episodes to achieve lower offline validation loss.*\index{Validation!data sanitization}

Suppose an archive of latch manipulation demonstrations includes human recovery maneuvers, and two separate policies train on competing subsets of this corpus. One policy trains on the full archive, including episodes where a human teleoperator backed off the gripper and re-aligned the jaws after the latch cam caught on the strike plate. The second policy trains on a sanitized subset stripped of all hesitation and retries, achieving a markedly lower loss on its held-out validation split. When deployed on the physical cell, both policies eventually encounter a misaligned cam. The first policy recognizes the contact anomaly, backs off, and seats the latch successfully. The second policy relentlessly drives along the nominal path, building contact force until the safety supervisor's force tripwire halts the cell. Because the sanitized dataset excluded off-nominal recoveries, the lower validation loss proves only that predicting smooth nominal trajectories is easier to fit than handling physical disturbances\index{Disturbance rejection!recovery data}. Pruning corrective demonstrations simplifies the loss score at the exact price of removing the feedback behaviors the physical controller needs off the nominal path. **Filtering out recovery trajectories to drive down offline prediction loss strips the policy of the corrective demonstrations required to escape compounding physical errors.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Retain all authority-record entries during dataset ingestion and admit, as training targets, only the stabilized, human-reviewed segments of attributable expert recoveries. Never prune demonstration corpora simply to minimize offline validation loss, and mandate closed-loop physical perturbation benchmarks to verify recovery competence before signing off on deployment candidate checkpoints.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Transitioning from human demonstrations to simulation reinforcement learning removes the failures training left in the policy.*\index{Reinforcement learning!regime transition failures}

An assembly team switches from behavioral cloning to simulation reinforcement learning to eliminate lateral drift during automated gasket seating. The resulting policy cures the drift in the virtual environment but commands joint torque oscillations at `{python} FallacyScenarios.f_chatter_str`. The physics simulator permits this aggressive chatter because its rigid-body solver assumes massless motor rotors and instantaneous torque reversal. On the physical machine, this high-frequency command excites drivetrain mechanical resonance\index{Actuation!mechanical resonance} and rapidly heats the motor windings toward their thermal trip point via $\TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance$ Joule losses\index{Thermal management!Joule heating}. The drive electronics throttle current to prevent permanent motor damage, causing the assembly stroke to stall before seating completes. Shifting training regimes solved an imitation drift problem by introducing a high-frequency chatter exploit that the simulator did not penalize. Qualification must therefore evaluate the full physical task under sustained cyclic operation, verifying simulator dynamics assumptions against physical hardware telemetry. **Switching to simulation reinforcement learning substitutes numerical solver shortcuts and unmodeled mechanical dynamics for human demonstration deficits.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Require paired-trace validation across all four reality gap channels before deploying simulation-trained policies. Enforce low-level hardware rate limiters and digital low-pass action filters ($\ActionFilterCutoffFrequency \le$ `{python} FallacyScenarios.f_cutoff_str`) within the embedded motor drives to suppress high-frequency chatter originating from unmodeled rotor inertia.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming online gradient updates preserve predeployment safety envelopes.*\index{Statistical verification!collapse under fine-tuning}

When a simulation-trained policy shows steady-state positioning error on a physical assembly fixture, an engineer might enable online policy-gradient fine-tuning directly on the robot. After `{python} FallacyScenarios.n_finetune_steps_str` gradient steps, the arm successfully eliminates contact positioning error at the fixture, prompting the team to declare the updated model production-ready. Applying parameter updates $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ directly to the policy network, however, produces an entirely new checkpoint with changed weights. The behavioral trials accumulated during predeployment qualification remain observations of the original checkpoint and do not establish performance of the updated one. Independent permission and fallback properties may remain applicable only while their plant, timing, authority, isolation, and realization premises hold; integration must check those premises after the update. While local contact accuracy improves, unconstrained backpropagation into shared representations triggers catastrophic forgetting in rarely visited state-space regions. As a result, the fine-tuned policy may lose stability during high-speed free-space slews or corrupt its emergency deceleration profiles. Because physical robot time and mechanical wear preclude repeating full-scale testing suites on hardware, regression suites must isolate and verify every operational envelope that gradient updates might perturb. **Online gradient updates require fresh behavioral qualification and reopen every assurance claim that depends on the changed checkpoint or execution conditions.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: When a bounded correction suffices, use gated residual policy architectures ($\NominalControlCommand = \pi_{\text{base}} + \ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\,\FiniteChange\Policy$) with an externally enforced binary gate ($\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState) \equiv 0$ in free space) to localize real-world adaptation. Mandate automated, frozen non-regression suites that verify trajectory tracking and stopping profiles before granting execution authority to updated parameters.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Believing that widening parameter distributions can substitute for missing physical mechanisms.*\index{Domain randomization!panacea fallacy}

When an assembly policy repeatedly fails on physical hardware, an engineering team might attempt to brute-force sim-to-real transfer by radically widening the simulator's domain randomization bounds. They randomize link masses by ±`{python} FallacyScenarios.mass_spread_pct_str` and vary surface friction coefficients across the extreme interval from `{python} FallacyScenarios.mu_lo_str` to `{python} FallacyScenarios.mu_hi_str`. On the physical test bench, however, the trained policy behaves poorly: it moves sluggishly through free space and hesitates indefinitely upon initial contact. Randomization perturbs coefficients exclusively within the governing differential equations already hardcoded in the physics engine. It cannot synthesize missing physical phenomena such as gearbox backlash, joint cable compliance, Stribeck friction, or sensor transport jitter. When dynamically incompatible virtual plants produce indistinguishable observations, a memoryless policy cannot choose separately for each plant; average-return optimization may favor a slow compromise or may sacrifice low-probability cases. While recurrent or history-conditioned architectures can adapt to wide parametric variations by estimating system properties online, even an adaptive policy cannot identify or compensate for physical mechanisms that never existed in its training simulator. **Expanding parameter randomization bounds merely shifts the probability distribution across existing simulator equations; it cannot synthesize unmodeled physical dynamics.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Calibrate baseline physics engine parameters against real hardware test fixtures before introducing domain randomization. Explicitly document whether parameter distributions derive from empirical instrument measurements or heuristic curricula such as automatic domain randomization. Enumerate known physical omissions, including transmission elasticity and actuator deadbands, in the policy manifest's omission log, ensuring that hardware-level safety watchdogs bound operations within verified modeling assumptions.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming multi-step generative decoders can execute synchronously within inner actuator control loops.*\index{Diffusion policy!inference latency wall}

Aiming to capture multimodal trajectory distributions observed in offline demonstration logs, an engineer replaces the single-pass ACT feedforward decoder in `latch-bc-01` with an iterative `{python} DecoderBudget.k_ddim_str`-step diffusion denoising head. The team deploys the new architecture synchronously into the robot's real-time inner control loop, scheduling a complete iterative sampling cycle for every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` actuator setpoint. Under the hardware inference budget evaluated in @sec-training-decoder-costs, executing all denoising steps consumes `{python} DecoderBudget.t_ddim_str`, exceeding the allowable control step deadline. Because the synchronous dispatch pipeline stalls awaiting model convergence, the system routinely misses setpoint deadlines. The low-level controller must either freeze on stale command setpoints or trip safety watchdogs on every iteration overrun. The weight-streaming floor of @sec-brain-memory-wall bounds each evaluation from below, and @sec-brain-action-chunking shows that re-reading the action head on every evaluation can dominate the decoder's cost; `{python} DecoderBudget.k_ddim_str` dependent evaluations each pay that floor, so the sum misses the setpoint deadline before scheduling jitter is even counted. **Deploying multi-step generative policies into high-rate actuator loops requires decoupling iterative trajectory generation from real-time setpoint tracking through asynchronous execution contracts.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Decouple iterative policy inference from high-frequency actuator control loops whenever measured inference latency approaches the control period. Formally partition the pipeline into an asynchronous planner generating trajectory chunks and an inner controller tracking them under qualified execution leases. Explicitly track prediction horizons, executed setpoint prefixes, and proposal renewal deadlines. Buffering trajectory chunks never grants permanent operational authority: the execution engine continuously validates physical safety invariants and triggers safe stopping profiles whenever a lease expires without a fresh proposal.

:::

## Summary {#sec-training-summary}

A policy's weights keep what its training experience rewarded and forget which experience that was, so each regime is best remembered by the dependency it leaves behind. Demonstrations leave a dependency on coverage: a point-regression head averages valid modes into an action no one chose, and even a multimodal head drifts into states the demonstrations never recovered from. A reward-labeled log leaves a dependency on the support of the logged actions, and a pretrained base on someone else's embodiment. Trial on the machine pays for its experience in calendar time, winding heat, and drivetrain life; simulation pays almost nothing per trial but inherits every approximation in its contact solver and every mechanism it omits; fine-tuning on the machine creates a new checkpoint that needs its own behavioral evidence and review of affected assurance premises. None of these dependencies shows in a validation loss or a simulated return.

Orthogonal to the source of experience, every policy must deliver its proposal inside the machine's deadline $\CompletionDeadline$. The decoder that represents several modes buys that representation with dependent evaluations, and what decides whether it can run is renewal slack against the jitter allowance, not mean latency. When slack runs out, the chunk lease, not the decoder, bounds how long an admitted prefix keeps moving the arm.

The policy manifest gathers these dependencies into one claim with stated limits. Its declared ODD is the supported cells of the data join minus every state the omission log excludes, never a region read off a training curve. For the latch, that rule sends `latch-bc-01` to evaluation at the nominal plate and the guarded approach, holds the simulation-refined checkpoints until paired probes bound the contact and timing omissions, and lets `latch-bc-recovery-02` carry a wider claim that new recovery experience has to earn. An admitted action crossing the causal boundary carries no guarantee beyond the evidence that qualifies it, and the load-bearing relations behind that evidence are collected in @tbl-06-key-equations.

| Equation                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | What it bounds or decides                                                                                            | Derived in                          |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|
| $\pi^*(\RobotObservation) = \mathbb{E}[\RobotAction \mid \RobotObservation]$                                                                                                                                              | The squared-error optimum of a point-regression policy, which lies between demonstrated modes                        | @eq-training-mse-minimizer          |
| $\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\DecisionProcessState, \RobotAction) = \Reward(\DecisionProcessState, \RobotAction) + \DiscountFactor\,\mathbb{E}[\PolicyHistoryActionReturn(\NextDecisionProcessState, \NextRobotAction)]$   | The value recursion that offline and policy-gradient learning estimate from samples                                  | @eq-training-bellman                |
| $\ProposerInferenceTime = \ObservationEncodingTime + \sum_{k=1}^{\DecoderEvaluationCount} \DecoderPassTime \le \CompletionDeadline$                                                                                       | Whether a decoder fits the setpoint step synchronously or the renewal period asynchronously                          | @eq-training-decoder-latency        |
| $\TrialCampaignWallTime = \TrialCount\,(\TrialRolloutTime + \TrialResetTime)/\ParallelRigCount$                                                                                                                           | The calendar of a physical training campaign, which rigs divide but wear does not follow                             | @eq-training-trial-wall-clock       |
| $\UnbrakedImpactForce = \SpeedAtDetection\sqrt{\ContactStiffness\,\Mass}$                                                                                                                                                 | The peak force of a mass coasting into a contact, which a soft penalty spring understates                            | @eq-training-impact-peak            |
| $\EffectiveSeriesStiffness = (1/\LatchPlateStiffness + 1/\RobotStructuralStiffness)^{-1}$                                                                                                                                 | The robot-side stiffness above which a coasting approach exceeds the latch limit                                     | @eq-training-series-stiffness       |
| $\ContactYieldDeadline = \LatchForceLimit/(\ContactStiffness \SpeedAtDetection)$                                                                                                                                          | The time from touch to the force limit under constant drive, which confines the declared ODD to the guarded approach | @eq-training-contact-yield-deadline |
| $\DomainRandomizationObjective(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{\SimulationParameterVector \sim \ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector)}[\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters; \SimulationParameterVector)]$ | Return averaged over the parameters a simulator models, never over mechanisms it omits                               | @eq-training-dr-objective           |
| $\NominalControlCommand = \pi_{\text{base}} + \ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\,\FiniteChange\Policy$                                                                                                                 | Where a learned residual may act, and so what the regression evidence must cover                                     | @eq-training-gated-residual         |

: **Key equations of policy training**: Each load-bearing equation of the chapter, the limit it bounds or the decision it settles, and the equation where it is derived. {#tbl-06-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Policy synthesis and sim-to-real transfer"}
* **Every regime leaves a dependency no training score shows:** Offline loss and simulated return reward compliance with training data and numerical solvers rather than real-world physics. Candidate model rankings frequently invert when transferred to hardware. When an operating condition violates an unmodeled dependency, it produces a predictable failure signature that identifies exactly which runtime monitor the permission path must enforce.
* **Mode choice and recovery are separate problems:** Point regression can average valid, mutually exclusive demonstrations into an unviable intermediate action, whereas compounding execution drift pushes the system into states that the demonstrations never sampled. Multimodal decoders resolve action ambiguity; targeted recovery experience and closed-loop data resolve distributional drift. Independent runtime limits remain mandatory for both.
* **Decoder latency must fit the proposal contract:** Iterative denoising and deep autoregressive evaluations substantially increase compute latency and memory bandwidth pressure. When a policy cannot generate actions within the synchronous deadline, asynchronous action-chunk playback requires a validated hardware lease and deterministic fallback behavior. An expressive action distribution earns no extra execution time at the actuator.
* **Training information must survive the sensor boundary:** Privileged simulation states, such as ground-truth contact wrenches or global object poses, accelerate training, but the deployed student policy observes only noisy onboard sensor streams. Observation histories disambiguate physical variations only when those conditions leave distinct temporal signatures. Model distillation never removes the necessity for hardware calibration and empirical transfer testing.
* **Randomization covers parameters, not missing mechanisms:** Domain randomization widens policy robustness across modeled simulator parameters, but it cannot bridge physical effects that the numerical solver neglects. Backlash, unmodeled compliance, and sensor transport delays remain absent regardless of parameter range, requiring explicit entries in the omission log and channel-by-channel probe characterization on hardware.
* **Fine-tuning spends wear and reopens qualification:** On-robot trials consume component life, introduce thermal stress, and generate wear that cannot be parallelized across separate test rigs. Behavioral evidence gathered for an earlier checkpoint does not qualify an updated model, and independent permission properties require an integration check of their unchanged premises. A gated residual architecture strictly confines where learned adaptations take effect, but the integrated controller still demands thorough regression testing and hardware-level execution limits.
* **A wider declared ODD needs new support:** The policy manifest records dataset digests, training hyperparameters, and unmodeled simulator phenomena, explicitly excluding operational domains affected by unverified gaps. Scaling simulator throughput or pretraining a foundation model adds no supported cell to the declared ODD. Broadening the deployment boundary requires attributable physical recovery data and rigorous closed-loop hardware qualification.
:::

The declared ODD is where the second law, endogenous data (principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}), becomes a field in a record. A policy chooses its next observations by acting, so the states it meets in service are not the states its training visited, and no regime in this chapter escapes that. Cloning meets it as drift out of the demonstrated tube, learning by trial on the machine meets it as calendar time and wear spent visiting the policy's own states, and simulation meets it as states whose dynamics the solver invented. The manifest does not remove the dependency. It writes down where the policy's own evidence ends, so that everything beyond that line is treated as a claim still to be earned rather than as competence the weights happen to display.

When a candidate looks better than its evidence, the useful question is which of its states were visited on this machine and which were only scored. A wider declared ODD is bought with experience that joins to new cells, and choosing a training regime is choosing what that experience costs: an operator's hours, a drivetrain's life, or a probe campaign that closes a simulator's omissions.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-training-history}

The mathematical foundations of modern policy optimization originate in classical dynamic programming. @bellman1957dynamic introduced the principle of optimality and the recursive decomposition that defines value functions, while @howard1960dynamic formulated policy iteration to solve discrete Markov decision processes. Parallel to dynamic programming, learning from demonstration developed along an empirical path in robotics. Pomerleau's ALVINN demonstrated early autonomous road following by training a shallow artificial neural network to map camera images directly to steering angles [@pomerleau1989alvinn]. ALVINN quickly exposed the vulnerability of pure behavioral cloning to covariate shift and compounding error: because the network trained exclusively on demonstrations from an attentive human driver, it never encountered the off-center heading angles produced by its own steering mistakes, leading to catastrophic departures from the roadway [@pomerleau1991efficient]. @ross2011reduction formalized this failure mode through the Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) algorithm, proving no-regret reduction bounds by querying an expert supervisor on the actual state distribution induced by the learner's policy. When demonstrations encompass multiple valid strategies, naive regression averages distinct modes into invalid intermediate actions. Mixture density networks [@bishop1994mixture] resolved this multimodality for low-dimensional outputs, and diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] generalized the approach to high-dimensional action trajectories, executing action chunks with receding horizons on physical manipulators.

Algorithmic reinforcement learning split into two primary branches: policy-gradient methods originating with REINFORCE [@williams1992simple] and value-based temporal-difference learning formalizing around Q-learning [@watkins1992q]. Both paradigms measure sample complexity in abstract environmental transitions, ignoring the physical costs of real-time execution. On a real robot, every trial consumes calendar time, strains mechanical linkages, overheats actuators, and demands human intervention for environment resets. Large-scale physical grasping campaigns [@levine2018learning; @kalashnikov2018qtopt] demonstrated that collecting hundreds of thousands of real-world interactions requires dedicated robot farms running continuously for months under heavy maintenance. To bypass this physical bottleneck, robotic learning shifted sample generation into simulation. Proximal Policy Optimization [@schulman2017ppo] established itself as the standard policy learner by clipping the update objective to discourage excessive policy drift. Simultaneously, physics engines co-located directly on hardware accelerators eliminated host-to-device communication bottlenecks, enabling thousands of parallel rollouts on a single workstation and delivering billions of simulated timesteps per day [@makoviychuk2021isaac; @rudin2022learning].

Simulated rollouts solved the sample-throughput bottleneck, but they elevated the reality gap into the central engineering challenge. Policies trained inside idealized physics often fail catastrophically when deployed against the unmodeled friction, latency, and compliance of physical hardware. Domain randomization addressed this discrepancy by treating the real world as an unobserved draw from a randomized distribution of simulated environments, perturbing visual features [@tobin2017domain] and inertial dynamics [@peng2018sim]. The OpenAI Dactyl project [@andrychowicz2020learning] showed that broad dynamics randomization paired with a recurrent policy could reorient a block in a dexterous hand trained entirely in simulation, while reporting the unsimulated failures of the physical hand, chiefly hardware breakage under load; its successor extended the approach to solving a Rubik's cube with automatic domain randomization [@akkaya2019solving]. Classical system identification [@ljung1999system] found new life inside neural pipelines through learned actuator networks that capture non-ideal actuator dynamics and drive compliance [@hwangbo2019learning]. More recently, generalist foundation policies trained across diverse robotic platforms [@kim2024openvla; @black2024pi0] use pooled fleet demonstrations to cross-train visual and motor representations. However, borrowing cross-embodiment data introduces unverified physical assumptions and subtle distributional shifts. The policy manifest introduced in this chapter provides the rigorous systems contract required to track these lineage dependencies, documenting simulation distributions, sensor bounds, and training assumptions so that hardware deployment can be audited and verified.

Six foundational works trace the trajectory from classical dynamic programming to modern sim-to-real policy deployment:

- @sutton2018reinforcement provides the definitive derivation of Markov decision processes, value functions, and policy-gradient theorems from first principles, serving as the core reference for the reinforcement learning formulations in @sec-training-rl-primer.
- @ross2011reduction establishes the theoretical bound on compounding error in sequential prediction, introduces the DAgger reduction algorithm, and outlines the recoverability assumptions that @sec-training-recovery-experience evaluates on physical robot hardware.
- @chi2024diffusionpolicy introduces score-based diffusion models for action sequence generation on physical manipulators, establishing the receding-horizon chunk execution and iterative denoising computational budgets analyzed in @sec-training-decoder-costs.
- @peng2018sim focuses domain randomization on unmodeled physical dynamics rather than visual textures, demonstrating that recurrent policies implicitly identify system dynamics across randomized friction, mass, and damping distributions to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer.
- @andrychowicz2020learning offers one of the most comprehensive engineering case studies of an end-to-end sim-to-real deployment, detailing the distributed training pipeline, dynamics randomization ablations, and physical maintenance challenges encountered while reorienting a block with an anthropomorphic hand.
- @ljung1999system provides the definitive treatise on classical system identification, detailing the input-output parameter estimation techniques, excitation design, and validation metrics that ground modern actuator modeling and paired physical probing.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From policy manifests to evidence"}
Twenty successful consecutive trials provide limited statistical confidence for a demonstration checkpoint whose manifest declares a single nominal cell and inherits none of the simulator's omissions. @Sec-evaluation takes the formal policy manifest as its contractual input. It opens with an illustrative campaign of twenty nominal door trials of `latch-bc-01`, the single cell its manifest declares, and evaluates the bound so small a physical sample can establish. It then evaluates `latch-bc-recovery-02` through nominal regression and displaced-plate trials to decide whether the new recovery experience earns the wider claim its manifest requests within the guarded approach.
:::
